speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No statistics for Quebec?

There are no statistics for
Quebec in this publication. I have no idea why. There are none for Newfoundland, either, for the reason I have already indicated. The complete figures appear in this book, and they make very interesting, but, so far as I am concerned, very sad, reading.
There is another interesting thing about teachers which those of Anglo-Saxon and French extraction should consider. What is the racial origin of the majority of teachers in our prairie schools? At the moment the greater number of the teachers in western Canada are of neither Anglo-Saxon nor French origin. Well, racial origin or language has nothing to do with one's ability as a teacher, but it is interesting to most of us in this house of those origins to know we are not doing our share in contributing recruits to the profession. Thirty per cent of those in the profession have expressed the

intention of not continuing in it. In most cases the parents of the teachers-I am talking now about the western prairies and British Columbia-are farmers and skilled labourers who sent their children to the normal schools.
I have had some experience as a high school teacher in a city. We discovered that our better students were not going to the normal schools. [DOT] These young people stated quite frankly that they did not expect to be able to maintain a good standard of living by following the teaching profession. This is a fact that must be faced. If we want good teachers for our children, we are going to have to pay for them. You cannot expect to get good men and women for nothing. You cannot expect a man to go out in Saskatchewan or any other province and raise a family and contribute to the welfare of the community on a salary of $800 a year. I do not want my children taught by that sort of person, that is if that salary is any true measure of his worth.
To come back to the matter in hand, aid to education has been given before, but only in the form of special grants which were paid because of emergency. As a matter of fact, most of these grants in aid of education have arisen out of short-term policies, some of which remained and some of which did not. We need a long-term policy on a permanent basis for this whole thing.
As I say, these grants emphasized some special phase of education, such as vocational training during the war. I could talk for a long time on the question whether or not things like that are education. What is education? It is a subject I will not tackle here.
Will my hon. friend permit a question?

I see the Minister of Labour is trying to interject. I do not agree that education is something that you learn in a technical school, that it is a quick course given to teach a person how to fly an aeroplane or to be able to shoot straight with a machine gun. That is far removed from what I understand education to be.

If some of us did not work with our hands, what would happen? My hon. friend says that you do not obtain education at the vocational school. Let me tell him that I have done fairly well with my hands.

I think the minister is confusing training with education. I have heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) say many things, and I have quoted him on
Education
various occasions, but I think one of the best things he ever said was that the man who was best fitted to assimilate education and appreciate it was the man who had worked with his hands as a boy on a Saskatchewan farm. So far as I am concerned, I am prepared to back that up one hundred per cent. Even if the Minister of Labour had said it I would have supported it.
At the moment I am speaking of federal aid for general education-and I said "general" education. The whole future of this nation depends upon the quality of that education. Far be it from me to detract from technical or vocational training, or for that matter from the federal grants in aid of university education. I am in favour of all these things. I hope the universities will receive grants; they are certainly in need of them, and they should have support from federal funds. I am pleased to note that the Saskatchewan university has been provided with a grant of $1,125,000 by the Saskatchewan provincial government in the budget for 1950-51. I hope the universities will receive federal aid, but I want it made quite clear that such aid should not be permitted to delay or divert our minds from the greater field, which in my opinion is education in general.
In conclusion let me emphasize that federal aid should be granted so that every child in Canada, irrespective of where he lives or of the economic status of his parents, should be guaranteed a minimum of education as of right; consistent, of course, with his ability to take advantage of that education. The greatest need of our age and for the future is that our children have an interest not only in their own province and in their own country, but in the wide community of the world. So far as education can help to fill that need, it is worthy of support by all the resources of this nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no thought of attempting to examine too strictly the exact wording of the motion now before the house. I believe its intention is clear. As I understand it, the purpose of the motion is to bring to the attention of the government, through a vote of this house, the desirability of equalizing educational opportunity across Canada. I concur in the aims and objects expressed by the mover of the resolution.
There is only one point in regard to which I suggest that some caution should be exercised. In supporting the motion the hon. member said that we have little knowledge of the situation in the different provinces. Without raising the point for the purpose of criticism, I wish to say emphatically that

Education
there is a great deal of knowledge available. For many years the Canadian Education Association, which is representative of every province-including	Newfoundland, even
before Newfoundland became a part of Canada-has been examining this whole field, not only from the point of view of abstract educational problems, but from the comparative point of view as well. I should be greatly concerned if the adoption of the resolution led to the creation of a further board or commission of inquiry. The Canadian Education Association is fully capable of dealing with the question of the comparative levels of education across Canada. It is composed of the technical experts in each province who understand exactly what the situation is today and what the desirable level would be in the years ahead. I mention this in the hope that the resolution will pass, that the government will act upon it, and that the government will then consult those who have been studying this very question for many years.
It has already been said that there is no idea that the adoption of the motion should be taken as suggesting any encroachment upon provincial jurisdiction. It is a good thing to keep that in mind. Undoubtedly the house should be most careful not to make any suggestion that would lead to any measure of encroachment upon the jurisdiction of the provincial departments of education over this field. This does not mean, however, that the provincial governments would not welcome a measure of support which would make it possible for them to carry out the general advancement of their educational programs.
I wish to support what has already been said, and to repeat that it is necessary to deal with this matter on the basis of the special requirements of the different provinces, because the aim should be not only to assist education but also to equalize opportunities for education in every part of Canada.
I think it is particularly appropriate that the resolution should come up at this time. Later this year there is to be a dominion-provincial conference. The problem of equalizing education in a satisfactory manner is one which requires effective co-operation between the dominion government and the provincial governments whose responsibility it is to direct educational programs in their respective jurisdictions. I hope that with the adoption of the resolution the government will then determine what can be done and will be in a position to deal with the subject when that conference meets later this year. I suggest, however, that no attempt be made to lay down any conditions as a qualification upon which

financial assistance would be dependent. If that is done, the purpose which the resolution seeks to achieve will be defeated, because the provinces most certainly will not welcome an indirect measure of control which they would not accept directly.
In considering this subject I think there are ways in which the dominion government can assist without of necessity limiting their assistance to such arrangements as may be made for ordinary educational facilities. To a great extent the qualifications of our teachers will depend upon the number of young men and women who can take university courses, and particularly those branches of university courses which will qualify them for teaching. There is a great opportunity for the dominion to assist in that field by extending the number of scholarships which will make it possible for young men and women to take university training of that kind. Scholarships already are being granted. The number could be greatly extended with advantage to every part of the country.
There is another field in which the dominion government can act directly to assist the general cause of education. Today in this and every highly developed country, research in the field of education, in medicine, engineering, pure science and the broad general field, is the very basis of our progress. Grants might well be made to assist in research under each of these headings, and also to provide sustaining scholarships, in order that young men and women who demonstrate special qualifications in any field of research may be able to carry forward their advanced studies in Canada; thus we would reap the full benefit of the education they receive.
From time to time we speak with regret about the fact that intelligent young men and women, who have had the advantage of our educational system in the public schools, high schools and universities, have left Canada and availed themselves of opportunities open to them elsewhere. It is highly important to the advancement of Canada that we provide sustaining scholarships at a level which will encourage young men and women of the keenest intelligence to stay here in the field of research, whether it be in education, medicine, science, or anything else. I do not think we should be satisfied unless we can say without reservation that all our children, no matter where they may live, no matter what the circumstances of their parents may be, have open to them equality of educational opportunity to the utmost limit of human ability. That should be our purpose; and as I interpret the resolution, that is its intention.

The more we spend on education the less we will spend on reform and on prisons. When we ask where the money is to come from-and that is a very sensible question -I suggest that we could probably save some of the enormous expenditures we are now called upon to make on prisons and reformatories if we spent an additional amount in providing educational opportunities in all parts of this great land.
That does not apply only to moral status; it applies also to the health of our people. No greater measure of personal security can ever be given our citizens than to implant in their hearts and minds the highest possible character and the highest possible personal standards. Moreover, the best security we can give against avoidable ill health is to impress upon our people a sense of social discipline and training which will prepare them, to the very limit of their ability, to meet the physical as well as the mental tests of life.
Today education assumes greater importance than at any time in the past. It has been said in this house during the present session as in earlier sessions, and as it will be said again, that we are in the midst of a world-wide struggle for the minds of men and women. We are. We are not in a cold war. War is war; and we are engaged in a war between decency and slavery. Toward the winning of that war, to which we have already committed so much of our national strength, a very basic preparation may be made in our homes, our churches and our schools. The character of our people, which our children develop at their mother's knee, when they go with their parents to church, and later in the great public institutions of learning, will very largely determine our success or failure in that so-called cold war. Education is the very foundation of our civilization.
I propose to support this resolution, as I hope others will, without too precise an examination of its wording, with the simple thought and hope in mind that the government will take those preliminary steps as a result of which they will be ready to join with the provinces in expanding equality of educational opportunity to every part of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution now before us calls upon the government to take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada through the granting of, financial assistance to the provinces for that purpose. Before proceeding further, may I commend the hon. member
Education
for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) on having again brought this resolution before us. I say "again" because last fall the same resolution was considered by the house for a very brief period of time. I commend the hon. member also on the skill and sincerity with which he presented his case.
When the resolution was before us last fall the time factor operated in such a way as to prohibit many of us from expressing our views upon this extremely important subject. While prevented from doing so on that occasion, however, we have taken advantage of other opportunities to extend our support to the general proposition under consideration. In fact last February my leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), was so much concerned with the importance of this subject that he devoted a substantial portion of his speech during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne to the question of federal aid to education. As a former teacher and a former minister of education in the province of Alberta, the hon. member was admirably qualified to deal with this subject in a practical and realistic manner.
On that occasion the hon. member for Peace River made two extremely important assertions. I am not going to undertake to quote them verbatim because I realize that would not be in keeping with the rules of the house; however, he said something to this effect. First, nothing can contribute more to the internal security of Canada than a broad, general understanding on the part of her citizens; and second, if democracy is to function successfully and yield the results the people want from the management of their affairs, there must be a high general level of educational achievement among the people.
There is much to commend itself to us in those two statements. As hon. members will realize, owing to its size, its widely varying resources and the productive abilities within its boundaries, Canada has many areas in which incomes are much lower than in other areas. The degree of prosperity varies very definitely from province to province, and indeed from municipality to municipality within the province. As I think my leader also mentioned in February, the bulk of the revenues from which the school districts must pay their educational costs come from taxation upon real property. The inevitable result is a wide divergence in educational opportunity, because within certain areas there is substantially less real property for the authorities to tax. In those districts where production is unusually low and incomes

Education
therefore are very small, certainly there is less opportunity for our boys and girls to enjoy the educational opportunity and educational standards that are essential to their welfare and to the welfare of this country. I am told that many of our local school authorities are obliged to raise more than seventy per cent of their educational requirements through taxation imposed upon real property in the community. One appreciates how small must be the over-all receipts from the imposition of taxes where the amount of real property is limited.
In assessing current educational costs one cannot but give some consideration to several important factors which have resulted in an almost skyrocketing spiral of educational costs within this country. I have been told that anywhere from fifty to seventy per cent of the budgets of many local educational authorities goes to pay the salaries of the school teachers. I know, for example, that within my own province we have seen a greater increase in the salaries of teachers during the past five years than during any other five-year period in our history. Speaking of rural areas only, the salaries of teachers have increased by an average of eighty-five per cent.
I mention that only to indicate how in one field alone the burden of educational costs has climbed so rapidly within our country. I want to hasten at this point to say, Mr. Speaker, that certainly I know, from quite a number of years of personal experience, taking into consideration at the same time the nature of the work performed by teachers and also the present-day cost of living, that the teachers of Canada are today disastrously underpaid. The $1,500 or $1,600 averages in my province, for example, in our rural communities represent [DOT] probably 85 per cent to 100 per cent increase since the thirties. But is there anyone here who would argue for one moment that even a $1,500 or $1,600 average for schoolteachers, even in the rural areas of any province in Canada, is fit, proper or adequate recognition of the outstanding services which they perform to the community and to Canada? Yet when I refer to those $1,500 or $1,600 averages, I am quoting averages which are substantially higher there than in a great many other parts of this great dominion. Considered in the light of the training which it is necessary and desirable for a teacher to have, taken into consideration along with the highly important nature of the services performed by a teacher, and taken in relationship to the incomes of other employee groups within the country, I would say that salaries generally are terribly low, disgracefully low.
[Mr. Shaw.)
One cannot but note the increased cost of construction and equipment of school buildings within the Dominion of Canada. I have no specific figures available; but in passing I might just mention the fact that in my own province, for example, in a period of three years, 1947-49, capital construction increased from $2-6 million in the year 1947 to $4-7 million in 1949. If one were to take the general capital cost of construction in the educational field, I think that those figures might easily represent not a 100 per cent overall increase in the number of units built in 1949, but an additional cost represented by an almost double cost of providing the same units which were being provided in 1947.
Speaking last February my leader suggested to the government that it might be advisable for them to set up a revolving fund out of which the educational authorities within the country might be able to borrow money at a low rate of interest for the purpose of constructing schools and equipping them. In my province a step in that direction has been taken. Only this year such a revolving fund was set up by the government of the province of Alberta. Any school district within that province is able to borrow up to 25 per cent of its authorized borrowing for the purpose of school construction; possibly I should have said "approved school construction". The local board is required to repay only one-half of the original loan and there is no interest payable on that sum. Payments are extended over a ten-year period of time. I mention that fact only as an indication of something that probably could be done by the dominion government in order to assist capital construction in many parts of this Dominion of Canada.
Only recently I was advised that the cost of school equipment, principally schoolbooks in libraries and the like, has advanced by approximately 40 per cent within the last five years. I realize that there are certain definite reasons for this, such as an increase in the costs of materials which go into these books, advances in wage rates, rising transportation costs, and the devaluation of the Canadian dollar in relation to the American dollar. This latter factor comes in there substantially because of the fact that a goodly part of the printed materials in book form which are used are printed in the United States; and the additional 10 per cent has to be paid because of the devaluation.
We may get another picture of what is occurring from another reference to my province, and I am making references to my own province because of the fact that naturally one would have more information about his own province than he would about the others,

Education
and because of the fact that for some years I occupied a position in the school-teaching profession in that province. Taking my .own province, in 1947 the educational costs were $19-9 million; by 1949 those costs had increased to $26-6 million. The provincial authorities there have been endeavouring to relieve the burden which is imposed upon the local district by accepting increasing responsibility for meeting the over-all costs of education. I am, however, the first to admit that this action has not been reflected too greatly in the local field because of the continuing high costs of almost everything that goes into education. For example, within a period of three years, my province has increased the grants to the local school district by more than 6 per cent, from approximately 21 [DOT] 5 per cent to 27-2 per cent, while at the same time trying to assume ever greater costs such as contributions to a teacher retirement fund, which in itself has jumped from $6,600 in 1939 to over $587,000 in this year, 1950. I point that out, Mr. Speaker, as showing the increase in the cost of education and showing that, even though the province may go as far as it can having regard to its responsibilities in the over-all field, most of our provincial governments are experiencing a great deal of difficulty in meeting the over-all cost of education.
I may just refer to this matter of school grants for a moment, and once again using my own province largely because of the fact that it is with that province that I am familiar. School grants in the fiscal year 1935-36 amounted to $1-39 million. By 1949 those had increased to $7-78 million; and I am not taking into account of course this figure of $587,000 which is paid into the teacher retirement fund. As far as my province is concerned this represents an increase in cost of approximately 2 per cent. While 2 per cent does not sound like very much, it is 2 per cent of a budget which is probably five times what the budget was in 1935. In dollars it represents an increase of almost 700 per cent.
Again, Mr. Speaker, within that province expenditures on education from income account increased from $2-4 million in 1935-36 to over $10-71 million in 1948-49, and in 1950 it will likely go to $11-22 million. That represents an increase from 13-3 per cent to 23-5 per cent. I am going to say this before someone else does. I recognize that the province of Alberta has been extremely fortunate as far as industrial development is concerned. However, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to refrain from saying that that sort of thing has not come just as the result of the passage of time or by accident. We have been extremely fortunate in having within that
province a government which I characterize as a wise government, and as a government which has pursued policies which have resulted in the rapid development of those great resources.
If a province like mine, Mr. Speaker, with its increased revenues resulting in part from the greatly expanded industrial development within the past two or three years, finds it difficult, how much more difficult must it be for so many of the provinces where a corresponding set of circumstances has not existed. If it is becoming a burden in a province like mine, what must the situation be in certain of our maritime provinces, for example? The mere fact that we have been able to do some of these things of course does not mean that other provinces should immediately undertake to do it too; but is there any reason why the children living in some of these other provinces should be deprived of that quality of educational opportunity which I think all hon. members agree they should have?
When my leader spoke in February he was criticized, not in this house, but by a publication which I have had to refer to before and am sometimes obliged to call a questionable publication, namely, the Farm and Ranch Review. I do not know why I should pay any attention to it; nobody else does. It is a publication which is the product of a politically ambitious, though hopelessly frustrated individual. In its March issue this publication states-I am going to read this first statement because it will reflect the mental turmoil of the editor.
Who is he?
A man by the name of Porter.
Marsh Porter?

Yes. Probably the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) knows him. He says:
Offhand, we can imagine nothing of less consequence to this society than a speech by Mr. Solon Low. the leader of the Social Credit party in the House of Commons.
I think that proves what I said previously, Mr. Speaker. That expression is nothing but the irresponsible product of a politically ambitious but hopelessly frustrated mind. I continue:
But when he asks the dominion government for aid for schools, we cannot resist calling his attention to the fact that he is talking to the wrong people.
It should have been directed to his party-liners in Alberta. This year the Alberta government's income from oil lands royalties will far exceed $30 million. This income from wasting assets should go into permanent capital assets.

Education
I am just going to digress at this point to remind you, Mr. Speaker, and the house, that not long ago when I spoke here I referred to this same publication and to the criticism of the government of Alberta contained in it for paying off a very substantial part of its provincial debt and saving the people of the province an additional $18 million a year which they would have had to pay in interest and carrying charges had not that portion of the debt been liquidated. This is the publication that criticized the Alberta government for having done that, and yet they come along with this, which they would like to think is a great display of wisdom. They begin by telling us that we should be giving consideration to the fact that our oil and gas are wasting assets, and that we should take the proceeds from them and put them into other permanent assets. We have always declared, as has the premier of my province, that we recognize these are diminishing assets; but had we listened to the editor of the Farm and Ranch Review we would never, even from the beginning, have looked upon the proceeds from this development as diminishing assets. They go on and say:
No finer program for building up Alberta could be devised than a province-wide government financed school construction project.
When this publication came out the editor did not know, even though the papers were full of it, that the government of my province had set up a very substantial borrowing revolving fund for the construction of capital assets in the educational field within that province. I continue:
The Alberta educational council has urged the Manning government to undertake just that. It, of course, will pay no attention to the A.E.C.
In view of what has been done already this spring I think you, Mr. Speaker, as well as I, could find the appropriate language with which we might describe that particular editorial. I realize, sir, it would not be parliamentary whether you thought of it or whether I thought of it. I continue:
Maybe it would listen to Mr. Low.
The government of Alberta undoubtedly heard Mr. Low when he was speaking here, even though they were a couple of thousand miles away, but obviously the local government with its representatives in the same building did not hear him, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to remind the house that not only did the hon. member for Peace River point out that federal assistance should be made available for educational purposes, but he went on and mentioned several ways or methods by which this could be done. He referred to the old Municipal Improvements

Assistance Act which, as I believe he said at the time, has been in mothballs for a long time. It was an act under which approved projects entered into by school districts and municipalities could be financed in part at least under this act on an interest rate approximating 2 per cent per year. Certainly that act, or something comparable with it, could be put into operation and we could assist materially in meeting the burden of heavy capital outlays by our school districts in the several provinces.
He also referred to the school trust moneys. This would affect Saskatchewan and Alberta particularly; but so far as Alberta is concerned they still have $12 million here which I say we could put up a very strong argument for as a province. We feel that it is ours even though in the stricter sense of the word it is not.
The interest from that money was to be made available to the province to assist in educational work. We believe that $12 million itself could be put into a revolving fund out of which money could be borrowed for capital construction. Repeating again what the hon. member for Peace River said, we cannot see any continuing justification for the heavy taxes at present imposed upon vans and school busses. In my own part of the country, as well as in other areas of Canada, we have endeavoured to improve the educational facilities by the centralization of service. For example, in a community we have found that we could provide certain advanced educational courses for our pupils, provided a number of pupils were brought in from certain areas, so that one school could be constructed and equipped, and the very finest of teachers available could be induced to teach. An ever-increasing number of vans and busses are being used to transport these children.
However, the federal government insists upon imposing heavy taxes on these vehicles. We have urged and continue to urge the removal of such taxes. Finally, we would favour a straight grant to the provinces. Personally, I would go so far as to say that special consideration should be given to the poorer districts, so far as those grants are concerned. We are not limiting the action of the federal government to those specific fields, but would be glad to approve any measure which in effect would have the result of granting assistance to each province for educational purposes, and thus have the result of improving the educational standards and granting greater equality of educational opportunity for our youngsters.

I should like to see a vote taken on this resolution. After all that is the best way to ascertain where we all stand in a matter of this kind. What I have said today has been said for my associates in the Social Credit group. Those are the things we have fought for; those are the things we shall continue to fight for. We realize the provinces should do all they reasonably can within this field of education, and we assert that Alberta, at least, has accepted its responsibility.
Before taking my seat let me say that we have always stressed the fact that the administration of education should remain within the provincial jurisdiction, where it is today. Moreover we cannot forget also that a number of precedents have been established for the type of assistance set out in the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at length, because I join with the hon. member who has just taken his seat in my desire to see a vote taken on this resolution.
May I first thank the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) for what he has done in introducing the resolution and giving the house an opportunity to discuss a matter of particular interest and importance to all Canadians. I intend to support the motion, and I shall do so with no apologies for having on many occasions stressed the necessity for economy. Economy is parsimony when applied too strictly to education, because expenditures in education pay dividends by way of good citizenship which do not flow from many other expenditures parliament must necessarily make.
I join with those who have preceded me in stating that while at all times provincial rights must be preserved and maintained, and nothing must be done that in any way would appear to be control on the part of the federal authority over education, jurisdiction over which rests with the provinces, the carrying out of this motion would in no way constitute interference either directly or indirectly with provincial jurisdiction in the broad field of education.
Indeed, as the motion reads it can be accepted in principle by all, irrespective of the desire of each of us to support the constitution in its entirety. The mechanics for the carrying out of this motion must necessarily be left to those charged with the responsibility of carrying it out. I know of no better summary of the situation in general than that given in November, 1949, by the Canadian Teachers Federation, as set out in a booklet issued by them and entitled "Federal Aid to Education". As a foundation for the
Education
argument I intend to advance I should like to refer to one or two of the submissions made in this brief.
It states that the Canadian Teachers Federation represents a membership of some 60,000 and that, taken with La Corporation Generale of Quebec, makes up 99 per cent of the men and women who are in daily contact with boys and girls in Canadian schools. It points out that the federation is non-political, is not unduly affected by special interests, and is independent of governments, both dominion and provincial. It is only fair to say, and properly, that the Canadian Teachers Federation has lived up to its responsibilities and its desire to build the best Canadian citizenship.
In the course of this brief it quotes from its representations made to the government in February, 1949. On that occasion it said, in part:
We believe that a straight per pupil capita grant would bring the greatest benefits compatible with the safeguards which certain provinces would require to guarantee that the federal government would not infringe upon their jurisdiction in the field of education. . . We do not overlook the possible additional assistance which the federal government may render generally through an extension of the research program of the education branch of the bureau of statistics or through grants earmarked for specific purposes.
Then it expresses the desire to work with any committee set up by the cabinet, and also with representatives of the provinces, to the end that a system may be arrived at mutually agreeable to the federal and provincial authorities. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) dealt with that phase of the matter and suggested-I believe properly-that the mechanics of the fulfilment of the motion might very well be left to the dominion-provincial conference which is to reconvene this fall.
It sums up in a general way the answer to the question so often raised, namely that federal help might be regarded as an invasion of provincial jurisdiction, in that it might imply control by the federal authority over education in the provinces. I believe the answer given in the brief is a conclusive answer to those who advance that argument, when it says:
Federal aid for education is a need bom of a shift in taxation. Meeting this need1 may involve fiscal control-safeguards in the spending of funds from the federal treasury-but not policy control.
In any plan of federal assistance it would be understood and agreed that the expenditure of funds by the government of Canada would in no way be deemed to confer upon any minister or official of the government of Canada any right of supervision or control over any school or educational institution with respect to which federal government funds are expended.

Education
I would go further and say that it should not imply either control of the plan or the use that is made of the moneys advanced. One often hears it said that private members' days are a waste of time, and sometimes the number of members in the chamber would indicate that there was ground for that belief. But I believe it is through the instrumentality of resolutions such as this that private members' days provide an opportunity to the private member to discharge responsibilities that might otherwise be denied him. When this matter came up last fall the minister spoke on October 19, as recorded on page 946 of Hansard. Before the Prime Minister had concluded, the debate was adjourned and as private members' days ceased to exist for that session the motion died the inevitable death that occurs when private members' days are done away with. The Prime Minister spoke quite shortly and tersely and used these words:
I am sure all hon. members have welcomed this opportunity of focusing their attention upon this assertion, one which certainly appeals to each and every one of us, that there should be across Canada the greatest possible degree of equality of opportunity for the education of our young Canadians, the Canadians of the next generation.
That is an expression with which we are all in agreement. Then the Prime Minister went on to say:
Whether or not the granting of financial assistance by the federal government to the various provinces could be arranged in such a manner as to avoid exercising any direct or indirect control over the field of education, which is essentially within provincial jurisdiction, is a question offering greater possibilities of controversy.
With all the respect that one must have for the opinion of the Prime Minister I find it difficult to follow him in those words. We have grants in aid in various departments of government, all without supervision or direction in any way as to the means of expenditure. If we accept the need, if we accept the desirability of equality of education in all provinces, if we believe that Canadian citizenship can be built up only upon the foundation of equal opportunity to all young Canadians irrespective of their geographical location, then surely there can be no objection to the acceptance of this motion. It does not state that there shall be control; it leaves the administration to the provincial authorities. It makes the declaration of agreement with the necessity of the government taking into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada. After the Prime Minister dealt with that phase of the matter, he took another means of postponing consideration of the motion when he said in effect that as the Massey royal commission was sitting parliament should wait until it had

brought down its report. So that there will be no misunderstanding of what the Prime Minister said I read his words as follows:
Hon. members know that, at the present time, there is a royal commission investigating the problem as to whether or not we are making the best possible use of the public moneys being expended for the promotion of the development of the aspect of national life in Canada which is not measured in statistical trade returns, or in dollars and cents, or pounds and shillings.
Then a little later:
It will certainly be a matter of months before we can obtain a report from that commission, and I should think it would be wise not to attempt to determine with any degree of precision how the purposes can best be served until we have had that report.
It js not a question of how the purposes can best be served because this motion simply declares the desire of the house that the government should take into consideration means for expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose. In any event it is for the House of Commons and parliament to determine this question. The Prime Minister recognized the desirability of having equality of opportunity in education for the children of this country. That is all there is in this motion. I do not suggest that there was anything intentional in the termination of private members' days after October 19 last year, but whether there was or not it certainly was completely effective in the postponement of any action being taken on this motion.
I hope that this motion will be voted on today. I shall not speak for more than ten or twelve minutes, because I will not be a party to denying this house an opportunity to vote on this important matter.
There is one matter to which I think I should make reference. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) pointed out that in the prairie provinces the majority of teachers were of other than Anglo-Saxon or French origin. I do not know what he had in mind when he said that. I do not think it is racial origin that determines whether or not a Canadian is qualified to teach in our schools and inculcate principles of democracy in the children of the present or the next generation. I know the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will join with me when I say that many of these young men, whose parents came to this country forty or fifty years ago, are carrying out the principles of democracy which so many of them displayed on battlefields all over the world during the recent war.

I wonder if the hon. member would let me put myself right in that regard? I agree with everything the hon. member

Education
has said. What I really had in the back of my mind was to blame people of Anglo-Saxon and French origin for not taking on the job. I quite agree that racial origin has nothing to do with the making of a good teacher, but it is a point of interest to us in this house who are mostly of Anglo-Saxon and French origin that our own people are not doing this job.

I thank the hon. member for indicating that he has the same view that others from the western provinces have in that regard. I am not going to say that 1 was much of a teacher myself because my career as one did not last very long.
I guess they found you out.

There wasn't enough money
in it for you.

No, it was not that. I did not intend to mention this, but the fact was that my clock was fast. During the time I should have been in school I was out shooting gophers. The inspector, the late Dr. Magee, came along and indicated that gopher shooting was not a part of the curriculum and at the termination of the short term my permit was not renewed.
We hear a good deal today about the Douk-hobor problem. The Doukhobors make good citizens; it is the Sons of Freedom who have not made good citizens and who show no signs of doing so. In the school where I taught there were five Doukhobor boys who constituted the majority of pupils in that school. Three of them became professional men. One became a leading artist and the fifth became a missionary. That is indicative of what happens under our public school system. Those Doukhobors were a good type and made good citizens. In the main those in the province of Saskatchewan do not belong to the Sons of Freedom who today hold the law in contempt and show no regard for the educational opportunities they have had. One hon. member has said that education of itself will produce good citizenship. I knew some of the Sons of Freedom whom we had in our province before they migrated to British Columbia. Some of them were well educated but nevertheless they did not become better citizens in spite of the educational advantages they had.
Every conceivable argument in support of the resolution has been advanced by the mover and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) today, as on October 19 last. Summarizing my remarks, and supporting the resolution as I do, I believe that the resolution will provide certain advantages. First it will provide an opportunity for
greater equality among Canadians everywhere in the matter of education. Second, it will make possible the raising of teachers' salaries so that the best men and women will be mobilized for service in the great profession of teaching. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) explained the meaning of his words a while ago. I feel that the teaching profession is so notoriously underpaid today, even having regard to recent increases in the last few years, that however desirous most young Canadians with the necessary educational advantages may be to remain in the profession the rewards are too low. The level of reward is so low that it is no inducement to remain in the profession to those who wish to advance themselves and secure the material advantages of life. Everything should be done which will assure increase of their salaries. That would be possible under advances made by the federal authority, although not earmarked for that purpose.
In the third place, it would enable the extension of a system of scholarships, to which reference has already been made. Within the last few years there has been a wide extension in the granting of scholarships. To my knowledge the finest example in the world of the granting of scholarships is the Scottish system. Recently I was reading Lord Shaw's views on the subject. At the end of his life he was able to name many of the outstanding Scottish people of his generation whose contribution to their country had been made possible by a system of national scholarships.
I feel sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will be the first to support the resolution on this ground if for no other. On the 24th of February, 1937, a private members' day, he introduced a motion in the house reading:
That, in the opinion of this house, following the practice already established in Great Britain and other industrial countries, the government should investigate the desirability of a system of national scholarships to be made available to outstanding students who are financially unable to continue their education, to enable them to secure undergraduate and (or) post-graduate training in our universities, university colleges, agricultural colleges and technical schools.
I should like to see the system -of scholarships extended. I know something of the results in the province of Saskatchewan. Some twenty-eight years ago the Masonic order established a system of scholarships in that province available to all regardless of religious faith or racial origin. The purpose was to provide worthy Saskatchewan students with advanced education conditional on their undertaking to teach in the rural schools of the province where the population was of

Education
other than Anglo-Saxon or French origin. That system went a long way toward the improvement of educational opportunities. Several of these young men of various racial origins are making their contribution not only in the research council of Canada but also in the bureau of national standards at Washington, and their opportunities for that wider field of service were provided as a result of the establishment of these scholarships in our province.
I was one of them.
I intended to mention that.
I did not know you knew.

Yes, I knew that. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) was one of those who received a scholarship, and utilized it in such a way that two of his former pupils, the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison) and the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), are now members of the House of Commons. The scholarship won by the hon. member for Saskatoon paid off in good citizenship in the house to which he and I have the honour to belong.
Having said that, I join in what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has said in support of the resolution. I feel sure it is worthy of the support of members in all parts of the house. It is a resolution on which there should be a vote, and it should not be talked out.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is only by accident that I find myself in a position to speak on the resolution at this time. The discussion that has taken place up to the moment is one to which I can take very little exception. One might agree with most of the things that have been said. There was one suggestion, however, made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), which makes it necessary for someone in the government to say something at the moment. Since I happen to be the senior member of the government present at this time, it becomes my duty to make some remarks.
It has been suggested by the last speaker that because this resolution was considered on the last private members' day last session, and so near the end of that day that it was impossible to have a full discussion or to have a vote taken, the same thing might be intended on this occasion; and the last remarks of the hon. member were an appeal to us to see to it that the resolution was not talked out. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is not the desire of the government to have it talked out. It is the desire of the government to

have a vote taken; but I am not going to agree that it is the desire of the government to have a vote taken on the issues which have been presented to the house this afternoon.
Most of those issues did not have very much to do with the resolution; and most of us could agree with many of the things that have been said. But I think we should read the resolution, and should perhaps accept the interpretation that was placed upon it by the mover rather than the interpretation it has been given by others. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said he was not going to quarrel too much with the wording of the resolution. I can quite understand that, for if he had started to quarrel with it he would have had to oppose the resolution, on the arguments he presented before he resumed his seat. Therefore I suggest that, accepting the interpretation of the mover of the resolution, when we vote upon it we do not vote on the question of whether or not grants should be made by the federal government to promote research in education, for example. The federal government has been making grants to promote research in education under all governments for many years. I was going to say that has been done since the time of confederation, but I have not checked the records back that far. At any rate the government has been making these grants ever since I have had anything to do with education or with politics, and that takes me back at least thirty-six years.
Most of the types of research grants that were spoken of were given freely to institutions of higher education right across Canada, where that kind of research work is carried on. Grants for research purposes in connection with soil surveys, for example, are given to universities and colleges of agriculture right across the country, to promote examination of the qualities of soils and everything that goes with that in relation to agriculture. Grants have been made to assist in the development of ways and means to better safeguard the health of the people of Canada. Those grants have been made to universities and medical and nursing schools. Those are educational. Grants have been made to all provinces to encourage the setting up of technical schools, which the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) said he did not have in mind at all. Many others

have had them in mind, and had educational grants of that kind in mind in discussing this resolution.
We already have that.

Yes, we already have it, and my hon. friend said that was not what he was talking about. Eventually I am going to get down to what he was talking about. He was not talking of the kind of grant given to technical schools to promote the development of that kind of education; he was talking about something else. From what he said I am quite sure he was not talking about the kind of research grants we are making already to universities right across the country. I assume he was not talking of the kind of support we gave, the universities during and after the war which made it possible for young men to come back from overseas and get an education which otherwise they probably would not have been able to get. All these things have been done; all these things are accepted, and we are going on with them.
Then I take for granted that he was not talking about those scholarships that were mentioned by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). Scholarships can be set up to promote education in various ways, and are set up more particularly to encourage people to go into that kind of educational work associated with research, technical pursuits and all that sort of thing. Scholarships are set up to encourage people to go into that work and devote their lives to chemistry, for instance, in order to make some great contribution to the health of our people. All these things are good. They are being dealt with in one way or another now. They all have to do with the promotion of that aspect of education about which, as I have always understood it, there has never been any question of the federal government doing something.
So I think my hon. friend got himself down pretty well to the elementary schools of this country, or if he went beyond those he was talking about what we might call the secondary schools. He suggested that teachers should be better paid, and that education in the different provinces should be more the same. If I interpret that in what I would consider to be proper language in relation to education, it seems to me it has to do with the curricula in the different provinces. I agree with much of what has been said to the effect that the educational systems of the different provinces are not entirely the same; but I would point out that undoubtedly
Education
the people in those areas think they should not be much more alike than they are at the present time. That is their view.

I know the minister wants to be fair, and I did state today that it was not my suggestion that the curricula should be interfered with, or that they should be uniform. I did not mean any such thing, and I do not think I said it.
I was being fair to my hon. friend, because I was not just emphasizing the two things he Sid say.

If I might conclude what I was about to say, I also used the words "grants in order to allow the various provinces to carry on the type of education in which they are at present engaged". Those were my words.

I was trying to avoid saying what I will have to say now. When my hon. friend rose he pointed out that he did not want anything done that would interfere with the curricula or that would interfere with the control of each province over its teaching staff, and so on. He did not want interference in anything which under our constitution the federal government cannot interfere in now. But in stating why this resolution was necessary and why it should be adopted he called attention to the fact that there are great differences in the curricula across the country. He called attention to the fact that teachers are paid much better in some provinces than in others. Then, just before he sat down, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), called attention to the same thing and pointed out that the province with the greatest financial ability to take care of its requirements of any of the western provinces, and with ability to do so probably equal to that of any province of Canada, was finding it difficult now to continue paying the present salaries. If that is the case, then I should like to suggest to him that probably if he were to follow the meaning of this resolution, if it has any meaning applied to that, when you average the amount right across the country and take the poorer provinces along with those which are better off, it might not have the result of increasing the salaries beyond the salaries that are now paid in some of the provinces.
May I just point out, Mr. Speaker, that I did not tie it to salaries; I tied it to the entire educational costs. I referred to salaries.
My friend dealt with the fact that their salaries were $1,200 to $1,500 and that they were higher than in other provinces.

I did not say that either.

Education
You had better read your speech tomorrow.
I said the average was $1,500 to $1,600 in rural areas.

That is higher still; $1,500 to $1,600 in rural areas; and he says they are finding difficulty in paying salaries on those levels in Alberta now. The hope is, from his argument, that after they have received this grant from the federal government, they will be able to improve upon that. That was the suggestion of the argument. I am simply saying this, Mr. Speaker: If the second-best-off province in Canada- and I will put it there rather than the top of the list-is paying better schoolteachers' salaries now than they can afford to pay, how are we going to increase salaries right across Canada by getting a grant out of the federal treasury that must come out of the pockets of all the people in all the provinces of Canada? That is one thing that I think we have got to have a little further look at. It is all right to suggest that we are not at the moment talking about spending more money in Canada. But if there is anything to the argument, we are talking about nothing else but spending more money in Canada: spending it for purposes that might be all to the good, but nevertheless it is more money.
That having been said and other things having been said, I think that again we should have a little further look at the resolution before us. I read the resolution a few moments ago; and I indicated that, as far as I could make out, the mover of the resolution was talking about elementary schools and possibly secondary schools; he was not talking about higher education where these grants for research and all that kind of thing are made. He was talking about the very thing that the fathers of confederation were talking about when they were discussing this thing back at the time of confederation. He was talking about the very thing that we have all been talking about ever since. We have assumed that the provincial governments must have the control over the curricula, over the salaries paid, over the hiring of teachers, over the education and training of teachers and all that kind of thing, in a country so varied as Canada is. Then when they came to the conclusion that separately these provinces could not fully finance a system of education or any of the other systems that they had been asked to finance, they decided that the proper thing to do was to give them a per capita grant, grants to take care of their public debt and grants to take care of the other things. They handed them that money and said "Do what you like with it".
Everyone who has supported this resolution this afternoon has been putting forth the argument that we should not put any strings on the money that we give to the provinces.
Except for one thing. What I did say was that the only control that I saw necessary was one control that would ensure that the money was spent for the purpose for which it was voted.
And that purpose is education.
Yes.
Then that is control.
Yes.

As a matter of fact, that is exactly what this resolution does mean. This resolution means that the government is being asked to give all grants to the provinces with this one string on them, that they must be spent for education. Then my friend has given the best demonstration we could possibly get of what members of this house would do if we did that. They would be saying that the curriculum of this province is not as good as the curriculum in that province. They would be saying that the teachers are not paid as much in this province as they are paid in that province. They would be discussing all these questions which he was discussing this afternoon. And I venture to say again that it is the very thing which the fathers of confederation were trying to avoid our having to discuss and which everyone since has been trying to avoid our having to discuss.
Having said that, I am not going to say that the federal government should not do anything more to assist in education across Canada. There has been a way and there is a way; and that way no one has found reason for changing up to the present. When we laid down the basis for grants that were to be made by the federal government to the provinces at the time of confederation, we said they were to be on a certain basis. If I remember correctly-and I am only speaking from memory; I have not discussed this question for a long time-it was about 1907 before we changed that basis materially. They called an interprovincial conference and they changed the level of those grants. Why did they change it? It does not matter whether it was in 1907 or one of the other years in that neighbourhood', but there was the first time when they changed it. And on the occasion when they did change it, it was because costs of these certain things had gone up; and because they had gone up and because there was much more of it to be done than had to be done before, they raised

Education
the grant. They did not say, "We are going to pay a grant to education; we are going to pay a grant to promote mining in a certain area". They did not say, we are going to pay a grant in order to promote this or to promote that, but they said, "We will increase the grant to the provinces." They paid the whole grant to them and then they left it to the provinces to determine how much of it they were going to spend on education and how much they were going to spend in other directions.
I have not any objection-and I am quite sure that there is not any member in the government who would have any-to the suggestion that was made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that these are questions that are going to be discussed next September. In the interprovincial conference that is to be held next September the question will be discussed as to whether or not the government of Canada should provide the provinces, through some means or other, with more money than they are being provided with at the present time. One speaker after another has been saying that he used to teach school. I myself taught school for ten years.
That is too long.

That is too long perhaps to teach school at the salaries that we had then; I agree with the people who have been arguing that point. But nevertheless I did teach school. I was minister of education in the province of Saskatchewan for a number of years just as the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) was minister of education in the province of Alberta. I may say that I never was minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan, but I was minister of several other things, and one of them was education. This question has been argued right back through the years. But every time it was argued we asked the people down here for more money. When I was there, we were getting about $4 million for all purposes. I think we are still getting that $4 million, although I have not had occasion to examine the records carefully. On top of that we are getting from the federal government somewhere between $13 million and $15 million of money paid into the treasury of Saskatchewan. There has never been a string put on it to say that they could not spend the whole $15 million for education if they wanted to. They have had that extra money. I presume that when they go to the meeting in September there is going to be an argument to the effect that the amount of money that has been paid to the provinces ought to be increased. I do not know whether or not the federal government is going to agree that it
ought to be. I do not suppose anyone knows or will know until the arguments are heard. I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) to the extent that, in a thing like this, the question as to whether we are going to change the whole system, under which moneys are made available for all purposes, to one of turning over a certain lump sum of money to the provinces and saying, "That is for education and for education only", is a question which should be considered in September. To come out and say: There is a certain sum of money; now that you have it we expect you to equalize your teachers' salaries with the salaries in every other province; we expect you to teach the same subjects in this school as are being taught in that school; we expect you to turn out pupils that have the same qualifications as in other provinces-that can only lead to trouble.
The minister is drawing a red herring across the trail.

If my hon. friend reads his speech tomorrow he will find out himself that he criticized the conditions that we have in Canada under which our students and pupils from different provinces are not coming out from our school with the same kind of education. I would just ask him to take a look at the house we have here, which is the result of the teachings of the educational systems of all the provinces in Canada.
I venture to say that if you were to take two lawyers, one from one province and one from another, and compared them, you would not find a lot of difference in their ability to deal with the questions with which they have to deal. I think you would find that true even of the chaps who taught school.
What about the Minister of Agriculture?

There is not so much
difference in qualification between those who sit in one part of the house and those who sit in another, or those who attended school in one part of the country and those who attended in another.

What about the Minister of
Agriculture?

When I was minister of education I did not agree that any other curricula or any other system was exactly right excepting the one that I was administering; but I have gone across Canada since then, and I had before that, and I found that each one of the provinces turned out a pretty creditable group of pupils from its schools; and if they have the opportunity to go through secondary schools, one group is just about as

Education
creditable as the other. If they go through the universities, pupils are turned out of equal ability from the different universities. For example, the other night I was invited over to my own alma mater dinner at the university of Manitoba. I found that we could muster quite a group down here who the civil service commission seem to think are pretty good people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: They cannot compare with the university of Toronto.

On another occasion I noticed that the university of Alberta was doing the same thing, as was the university of British Columbia. On each occasion it was found that you could get just about the same number from one area as from another. In addition you found that one group was just about as competent as the other.
As I go around, the only thing I find in my experience is that quite a number have wandered from the maritime provinces to the other provinces, and they seem to get back here by some means or other. Quite a large group of them have graduated from our different universities, but they had their birth down in the maritime provinces. Everyone in this house knows why that is. Down in the maritime provinces they have had some difficulties in establishing industries and other things that are necessary, and large numbers of their population have shifted further west; but it does not make any difference where they started in the elementary schools or where they got their secondary school education or their university education, when they come into this house or into the civil service at Ottawa one group measures up just about as well as another.
For that reason I say there is no use discussing this question from the point of view of making us all alike. If we were all alike perhaps we would not agree as much as we do now. As a matter of fact we agree only because we understand the situation in the area of the country from which we come. We realize that because we have some difficulties there, other people will have difficulties in their areas, although they may be different from ours. But the men who have been trained in the secondary schools and the universities of the different areas are able to represent their point of view and what the difficulties are in their areas just about as well in one section as in another.
I say that for this reason. I agree with what the leader of the opposition said, namely, that the proper place to discuss this question and bring it to a finality as a matter of decision is at the September meeting. I do not see any reason why there

should be any great change in the method by which an additional amount of money is handed on to the provinces to be expended. If they are to have control over the expenditure of that money they will surely use a sufficient portion of it to take care of education. Therefore I think that is the time to consider the whole question.
On the matter as to whether or not it is going to interfere with the constitutional relationship between the provinces and the dominion, my suggestion is that we keep this as far away from that discussion as we can. I know of only one way of keeping away from a discussion and at the same time doing the thing that ought to be done, and that is, to make these grants, whatever grants we are to make, to the provinces without tying a string on them and saying: "You must spend this on education; you must spend this on something else." But say: "Here is the money. You know your problems; you understand what ought to be done." When we are speaking from time to time in this house we may say that one province is not spending enough on education, but they will probably tell us that it is none of our business, and they will go right on spending the money as they think it ought to be spent.
If we are to keep our people agreeing with one another across the country and cooperating in doing the things that ought to be done, we had better leave that question pretty well where it is. Since that is the question that the mover of the resolution says we are really dealing with, namely, a discussion of the question as to whether we are going to provide a grant earmarked for education, and thus introduce a discussion every session of the expenditures- whether or not they are being properly spent in order to do this or to do that-I say we had better leave that alone. If we are to pay an extra amount of money let us pay it in a general grant as always and say to the provinces: "Go ahead as usual and spend it." I am going to oppose the resolution.
