The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Knight:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) leading the government today has made it clear that he is opposed to the resolution. I presume that is a summons to all members supporting the government to rally against federal aid to education.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He said just the opposite.

By the time the right hon. gentleman had finished I had to read the resolution again and recall some of the speeches made this afternoon, because it seemed to me that the resolution itself had been changed beyond all recognition, and that after the description given them by the right hon. gentleman some of the speeches made this afternoon were scarcely capable of recognition.
However, I go by the terms of the resolution-and they are perfectly clear-and also by statements made by hon. members participating in the debate, and not upon the secondhand rehashing of them by the Minister of Agriculture to suit his own purposes in the debate.

Education
This is not a new resolution. It was before the house on October 19, at the last session, and appeared in identically the same form as we have it today. It is unfortunate that at that time little opportunity was given for debate. It came on a Wednesday afternoon, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself rising at about ten minutes to six and speaking briefly. The matter was not permitted to come to a vote, nor was it permitted to come before the house again at that session.
For my part I welcome the opportunity afforded the house today to pursue debate on this important subject, and I am very happy indeed to hear the Minister of Agriculture, speaking for the government, claim that he hopes to see this resolution brought to a vote today. I cannot think of anything that would be a more healthy occurrence in respect of this resolution than that it should come to a vote. And because I want to do all I can toward contributing to bring this question to a vote today, I shall be brief in my contribution to the debate.
The situation has changed only in two respects since the resolution was last debated on October 19. First, there has been evident in all parts of Canada a greater measure of support for the idea inherent in the resolution than had been apparent even up until that time. The second fact is that, if the deliberations of the Massey commission have any relevance, then presumably we are six or seven months closer to receiving the report from that commission than we were when the house debated this resolution last October. I am not suggesting that the fact that the Massey commission is sitting is a circumstance relevant to the debate at all. I mention this only because the Prime Minister in his brief contribution to the debate on October 19 cited that as a reason why apparently he did not wish to see the subject brought to a vote at that time.
I followed the Minister of Agriculture today with no little interest, and I shall attempt now to do that which he sought to do with reference to speeches preceding his speech in the debate, whfen he proceeded to state the substance of those speeches. The substance of the speech of the Minister of Agriculture, it seems to me was this, that what is being done now by the federal government and what is being done by provincial administrations in support of education is in all respects good and in all respects sufficient, and that therefore there is no occasion for any change in the present arrangement. With that statement I am in complete disagreement.
It is your statement, not mine.

The situation is not satisfactory at the present time. It is a misleading kind of artifice in a debate, and a resort to adroit strategem by the right hon. gentleman when he says, "Now, here are the products of the educational system of one place, and here are the products of the educational system of another place; they are just about equal when they get down here." Well, it is a very different thing to compare the qualifications of the graduates of various universities from comparing what is really a proper matter for comparison in this debate, namely the educational opportunities for young Canadians across Canada, from coast to coast.
If ever there was a fine example of drawing a red herring across the trail, then certainly the Minister of Agriculture today has drawn the biggest red herring across any trail that has been seen in this House of Commons for a long time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And that's saying something, too!
You are turning Tory, again.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The minister was referring to the hon. member sitting to the left of the hon. member who has the floor.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I can still tell a red herring when I see one; and that one really smells.

When anybody sees the light, the Minister of Agriculture should have no objection to people coming out of darkness into light.
The minister sought to suggest that there was some veiled assault upon the autonomy of the provinces in this resolution. What could possibly be more absurd! Everyone who has spoken in the debate this afternoon has prefaced his remarks with the clearest intention to maintain the exclusive legislative jurisdiction in the provinces in respect of the field of education and the institutions connected therewith. No member of the house has proposed directly or indirectly, by statement or by inference, that there is any thought whatever in the resolution of subtracting one iota from the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the provinces as it is set out in section 93 of the British North America Act.
Certainly it was not a situation calling for the kind of comment that fell from the lips of the Minister of Agriculture. Apparently when he has a weak case the minister, in attempting to buttress that case, comes along with the suggestion-he does not come right out and say so-that somebody is doing something or proposing something in the debate which is in fact the very antithesis of what they have said their intentions were.

Education
Let there be no red herrings from the Minister of Agriculture or any other member of the government on this issue. There is nothing in the resolution that in the slightest degree tampers with the legislative and administrative autonomy of the provinces in relation to education. Jurisdiction in respect of that subject was placed in the provinces by the British North America Act. There it remains, and there it will continue to remain, even if this resolution is accepted today in the House of Commons-as I hope it will be. No one can seriously suggest that there is the slightest intimation in the resolution of any attempt to dictate to the provinces in matters falling within their legislative jurisdiction.
The Minister of Agriculture introduced one further proposal when he said, "This is not the time or the place for a discussion of the question of federal aid to the provinces in matters of education. Reference has been made to the fact that there will be a dominion-provincial conference this fall. That is the place and that is the time to discuss this matter".
Well, that is a new one, coming from the government benches. We did not hear that from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) who is taking such an animated interest in this debate this afternoon. It will be remembered that there was quite a debate earlier this session on a resolution introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to deal with the subject of old age pensions and the setting up of a committee. Mention was made of the fact that that was a subject that might well come before the dominion-provincial conference this fall, but that was not treated by the Minister of National Health and Welfare as a reason why that subject should not be discussed in parliament or in a parliamentary committee. On the contrary, the minister seemed to give considerable encouragement to the idea of the discussion of that subject in a parliamentary committee, if I correctly understood him.

I extend to the minister my condolences. Here we have these two apostles of an outworn political philosophy sitting side by side at the moment and looking reasonably friendly. But in their expositions of the content of that outworn political 55946-1721
philosophy they seem to arrive at precisely opposite conclusions on similar propositions of fact. Here is the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), if you please, who says that parliament is not the place and that this is not the time to discuss the subject of federal aid to education.
I did not say that at all. Discuss it all you like. I told you how I was going to vote.

I am sorry if I misunderstood the right hon. gentleman. As I understand it now, he, speaking for the government and that vast phalanx over there, says he is going to vote against it and therefore there is no use parliament going on to discuss it. That is a new idea of the autocratic and totalitarian philosophy of the government opposite. Either the Minister of Agriculture is completely at variance with the Minister of National Health and Welfare and with common sense, or he has expounded and in fact is' asking the house to subscribe to the simple authoritarian proposition that when the Acting Prime Minister or the leading member of the government of the day says that he is going to vote against a particular resolution then parliament ceases to be the place to discuss that question. Not being able to follow these authoritarian minds in their various processes I still believe that, notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Agriculture considers that he has doomed this resolution to the limbo of defeated resolutions, this parliament still is the place and this is the time to discuss this matter because it is a matter of great importance to people in all parts of Canada.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare said that there should be an expression of opinion on the part of parliament on a subject in which he was interested and which certainly is bound to come before the dominion-provincial conference, but the Minister of Agriculture by way of contrast says that because he has spoken on this subject he has sounded the death knell of the resolution, and because this matter is coming before the dominion-provincial conference then this is not the place and this is not -the time to discuss the subject. The Minister of Agriculture can have his authoritarian and totalitarian philosophy all to himself and let him get what comfort he can out of it before the democratic-minded people of this country catch up with him.
What is at issue in this debate? The aim of the resolution is the equalization of opportunity for all young Canadians across Canada as far as education can do it. It will profit the Minister of Agriculture very little to deny that that is inherent in this resolution.

Education
If he does I can quote him an interpretation of a resolution in identical terms by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who spoke on October 19, 1949, as reported on page 946 of Hansard. At that time the Prime Minister said:
I am sure all hon. members have welcomed' this opportunity of focusing their attention upon this assertion, one which certainly appeals to each and every one of us, that there should be across Canada the greatest possible degree of equality of opportunity for the education of our young Canadians, the Canadians of the next generation.
The Prime Minister recognized what was inherent in that resolution. The Prime Minister saw quite clearly that which the Minister of Agriculture has so effectively sought to becloud. What is proposed here and what is the whole purpose and intent of this resolution is to achieve for young Canadians right across Canada equality of opportunity as far as education can equalize opportunity. Let us be quite candid and realize that equality of educational opportunity cannot achieve complete equality of opportunity for young Canadians. I suppose in only a theoretical sense will it ever be possible to have complete equality of opportunity in a world inhabited by humans, but educational opportunity, if it adheres to the principle of equalization, will do much to afford to young Canadians, regardless of the means of their parents and of the section of the country in which they happen to be born and raised, equality of opportunity with other young Canadians.
It is not simply a matter of equalizing opportunity as between the provinces, although that is involved in this resolution as far as it can go. But it does involve the seeking by proper and constitutional means to effect as between individuals that equalization of opportunity so far as it can be brought about by educational opportunity. Apparently the Minister of Agriculture is entirely satisfied. He looks around at the persons coming from the different provinces-he is careful to select those who have had the benefit of higher education-and he says, "All is well". I am sure the minister must have had experiences similar to those I have had, but I think he has forgotten about them.
He and I were born in places about ten miles apart. While I did not have much of my formal education in the county in which the minister and I were born, nevertheless he got quite a bit of his education there. Let us agree that he has made good use of it. When he was growing up he must have seen many youths, as I have seen in my shorter span, who by reason of lack of means on the part of their parents were denied the opportunity of higher education. They were denied not just

university education, but in many cases even high school education. Many of those youths I knew might have made just as good use of that educational opportunity as I did, or perhaps even better.

Thank you. I tried to take advantage of what educational opportunity was afforded to me, but I should like to see every young Canadian given the same educational opportunity that I was. It was not done without considerable sacrifice on the part of my parents, and I want to make it perfectly clear that there will always be a place for young Canadians to make sacrifices in order to attain the advantages of education. But much can be done that has not been done to afford educational opportunity to young Canadians who are being deprived of such opportunity today, an opportunity of which they could make the most excellent use but an opportunity which they are denied by reason of lack of means on the part of their parents.
This problem has gone far beyond the means of local governments. There has been no little improvement in the scale of salaries paid to schoolteachers in recent years but much of it has been due to the greater assistance afforded by provincial governments. Many provincial governments are today in the position where they cannot go much further in affording assistance in the field of education. That is the reason why aid is required on a constitutional basis from the federal government to assist in providing educational opportunities.
We have made great strides in the field of education in Canada. There is no need for envy when comparing the educational systems existing in the provinces of Canada today with those in other parts of the world. Canada can boast of having given to the world men who are leaders in the field of education, and who can hold their places with teachers and educationists from any other country in the world. There are great benefits to be derived from education. We have good systems in Canada. It is necessary though that aid be given to extend the benefits of those systems to those who are not in a position today to take full advantage of the educational opportunities that our provincial systems are intended to afford.
I wish to express my profound regret that the acting leader of the government, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), has seen fit to expound so reactionary a point of view as he did this afternoon. In effect he says:

Mr. Speaker, we were discussing the following resolution:
That in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
I doubt whether anyone in this house can speak with authority on whether or not education, from the eastern boundary of our country to the far west, needs financial assistance. It is because of that fact that I do not intend to speak on the educational facilities throughout Canada. I do know something about the local situation in British Columbia, having served on a school board there as late as June, 1949. Because I know of the conditions that prevailed at that time in my own riding, I intend to speak of that situation.
Education
During the latter part of 1949 and the early part of 1950, about 70 families per week entered the constituency of Burnaby-Richmond. This meant that approximately 135 children came into the riding every week of the year. With 30 to 35 children in every classroom, this meant that between 4 and 5 classrooms per week were filled. I know what financial stress that put on the riding, and because of that I am going to attempt to link up the financial situation in Burnaby-Richmond with federal aid for education.
Over a long period of time, and. by process of bylaw, we were able to build some schools. In fact, the riding now has about a dozen more, but the result of that put my riding into the hands of the receivers. For some years the constituency was handled by one man until those debts were paid up. Today, through the grace of a good provincial government, we are able to run our own affairs, because that government is putting approximately $35 million per year into education. I believe that is more than the total amount the province of British Columbia should pay to educate our children. Our position on the west coast is perhaps a little different from that of other provinces, because of the increased migration into British Columbia from the prairies and Ontario. In the end, people realize that British Columbia is the ultimate so far as living in Canada is concerned.
During the next five or six years our schools will be overtaxed no matter how we try to keep up with construction. In educational circles it is felt that 30 pupils per classroom is about the number any teacher can possibly handle. In Burnaby-Richmond the average is something like 45 per classroom; at least that is what it was when I left. It has reached the point where no province or municipality can contribute further towards education. When we loaded the elementary schools there was a blank space at the top end. We loaded our high schools with pupils who should never have been there in the first place. Many of the teen-agers going through elementary and junior high schools should never be there, because almost 50 per cent of them do not intend to attend a university. Many of them will not have the financial means to do so. It has been found that most of those pupils should go to vocational schools; that is their proper future. The other 50 per cent-I think that figure is exaggerated-should have the opportunity of ascertaining whether they can get the required marks that will enable them to go to university. Of the 50 per cent who should go to high school, perhaps 10 per cent have parents who can

afford to send them to university. What about the other 40 per cent? I think this is where federal aid for education comes into the picture. This 40 per cent of our young men and women attending high school have parents who are not financially able to send them to university. I believe it should be the ambition of the federal government to inaugurate a series of scholarships that would allow our teen-agers to go to university, should their marks come up to the required standards. I am going to support this resolution, because I believe it is aimed at assisting these teen-agers who are attending our high schools.
Many of the speeches this afternoon have gone far beyond the point the member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) intended when he introduced the resolution. I intend to support the resolution because I know that, from the practical standpoint, these young men and women in our high schools who deserve to get a university education are not getting it, because provincial and municipal finances will not allow further aid to education. This afternoon it was said that a lawyer from New Brunswick is just as good as a lawyer from British Columbia, and that a schoolteacher from Nova Scotia is just as good as a schoolteacher from Alberta. I do not see the point of such a statement. I do not think that is what the member for Saskatoon meant when he spoke of equalization of educational opportunity across Canada. I believe he meant an equal opportunity for education for everyone who desires it. Because I believe that, I still want to refer back to these young men and women who are attending high school. When hon. members are speaking tonight, or when they are voting, I wish they would remember that their vote will either help these young people or allow them to remain in high school until grade XIII, at which time they will go out into the world with nothing more than senior matriculation, and that does not mean very much in this day of specialization.
I want to put the cost of education in British Columbia on the record, Mr. Speaker. Within the last few days the provincial minister of education gave me the figures, and for the school year 1946-47 the cost was $20,100,000. In 1947-48 it rose to $25,750,000; in 1948-49, it was $35,500,000. The provincial share of those total costs was as follows: 1946-47, $9,500,000; 1947-48, $12,500,000; and in 1948-49, over $17 million, which is approximately 15 per cent of the total budget.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that no province can stand that strain on its financial resources without some help from the federal government. I believe too that without that federal

help the municipality of Burnaby will again be in danger of going into receivership in the near future. Although we have a good municipal administration in that district, with the strain of the cost of education on Burnaby-Richmond at this time, I do not think it is humanly possible for the council to bring to fruition the educational ambitions of our people. I intend to support this resolution.

When the history of this century comes to be written, Mr. Speaker, the one theme that will run through the story of the first half of it, and possibly through a large part of the second half, will be the struggle of the democratic world against dictatorship. History will record how, in the first half of this century, the democratic countries fought two world wars to preserve their way of life, to preserve democracy from being overthrown by dictators. It will record how at the present time, in these years, democratic countries including our own are spending up to half of their government revenue in order to maintain their defences against dictatorship. When that history comes to be written it will show that the one great ally on the side of democracy, the one ally that will in the long run help to preserve democracy, is education. Writing on the subject of education, Horace Mann, who is known through the world as one of our greatest and most progressive educationists, has this to say:
If ever there was a cause worthy to be upheld by all of toil and sacrifice that the human hand or heart can endure, it is the cause of education. It holds the welfare of mankind in its embrace as the protecting arms of a mother hold her infant to her bosom. The very ignorance and selfishness which obstruct its path are the strongest arguments for its promotion, for it furnishes the only adequate means for their removal.
Those of us who believe in democracy and are concerned to see our way of life eventually succeed over dictatorships cannot but be concerned about the whole question of the education of our citizens. In the modern world, dictatorships today rely on terror methods, on a controlled press, on the denial of information to the people, and on the subordination of the thoughts and actions of the masses to the purposes of ruling cliques or individual despots. On the other hand, democracy rests on the emancipation of the human spirit, on individual freedom, on education for private living and for social participation. The character of our citizenship is determined to a great extent by the nature of the education which those citizens receive.
As has been said already in this debate, while education in and of itself does not make good citizens, nevertheless outside the home and the church there is no greater

agency in this country for helping to build citizens than that of our schools. The character of Canadian citizenship is, apart from the home and the church, basically fashioned in the schools of the nation. When we speak of citizenship being fashioned in the schools of the nation, we think first in terms of the elementary school; second, in terms of our secondary or high schools; and only third, in terms of our centres of higher education or universities. The elementary school is basic; it is the first and most important of all. One reason for that is that there are still many thousands of our children who never get beyond the upper grades of the elementary school or who at best never get beyond the lower grades of the high or secondary schools. The elementary school is the one centre that our children who attend school at all have an opportunity of attending. In the second place, it is in the elementary school that the children are passing through their formative years. It is then and there that the foundation of socially approved attitudes and of good citizenship are firmly laid, if they are to be firmly laid at all.
It is because of the importance of education in a democratic country, because of its importance to the very survival of democracy in today's world, that education down to the level of the elementary school must become the concern of our federal parliament. No federal parliament that has any understanding or appreciation of the vital importance of education to the survival of our way of life can afford to let any question either of jurisdiction or of economy stand in their way in this vital matter.
Since the foundations of good citizenship are to be laid in our elementary schools and reinforced in our secondary or high schools and our universities, every province in Canada must be financially capable of providing teachers of high personal qualifications and extensive training. To the men and women who are to do this job which is so fundamentally vital they must be in a position to offer remuneration in line with that which is offered by commercial and industrial concerns. It is far more important to the wellbeing of this nation that we have capable and adequately-trained personnel in the classrooms of our schools than in our offices and factories. It is a national calamity that only second-rate and partially-trained personnel, paid third-rate salaries, is often all that can be secured to staff these classrooms in which such a vitally important job is to be done.
Education
It is a national tragedy that that should be the situation in so far as our schools are concerned, whilst industry and commerce, where visible monetary profits prevail, can outbid school authorities at every level in securing at much more remunerative rates the best trained and most capable personnel. And even more deplorable than this is the fact that nowhere in Canada can educational authorities compete with industry and commerce in remunerating their personnel. More deplorable than that is the fact that such educational opportunities as are being offered to the children of this country vary, as has already been said, very widely from one municipality to another and from one province to another.
The disparities in ability of individual provinces to supply and equip suitable buildings, to train and pay suitable teachers, to provide suitable programs of diversified education are all too well known, too widely recognized to require elaboration. By and large in this country today the educational opportunities afforded to children of any province can be measured in the amount of money per pupil spent by that province on education. There are other factors, but as a rule the best measure we have today of the quality of education that our children are getting in the various provinces is the amount of money that these provinces are paying per pupil. What is also true is that expenditure in the Canadian provinces varies very directly with the individual or personal income of the people of that province. I will give figures for 1946, the last year for which I have them. In 1946 Prince Edward Island had an average personal income, based on the school population, of $3,000. In that year that same province, which had the lowest personal income per pupil of any province of Canada, also spent the least money per pupil on her schools. In that year she spent $45 per pupil on education. In the same year British Columbia spent $115 per pupil as against Prince Edward Island's $45, nearly three times as much. Notwithstanding the fact that Prince Edward Island spent only $45 and British Columbia spent $115, both provinces made practically the same effort on the basis of that income.
British Columbia spent on education $1 out of every $63 of personal income received. Prince Edward Island spent $1 out of every $68. Here were two provinces each putting forth practically the same effort, paying the same percentage of their income on education, one province able to provide $45 per pupil, the other with no more effort on their part able to pay $115 per pupil.

Education
In the same year, making another comparison, New Brunswick spent $1 out of $53 personal income, and Ontario spent $1 out of every $55. In that year and on that basis Ontario was able to pay $116 per year per pupil on education; while New Brunswick, making the same comparative effort, was able to pay only $60 per year per pupil. To give a still further illustration in the same year, Saskatchewan paid $1 out of every $34 personal income on education; Alberta $1 out of every $36. Their sacrifices or their efforts based on the personal income of their citizens were almost the same, yet these provinces were paying slightly less than either Ontario or British Columbia who were paying $1 out of every $55 and every $63. Here were two provinces paying $1 of their personal income out of every $34 and $36 and yet they were not able to spend on education on that basis as much as Ontario and British Columbia were spending, who were spending only $1 out of $55 and $63.
If as a nation we in Canada are to pay anything more than lip service to the democratic principle that is involved in the term "equality of educational opportunity", then we must find some means whereby educational facilities in the smaller and poorer provinces can be raised to a level that is suitable to the whole of Canada.
It is not necessary that the education should be uniform. No one who believes in federal aid for education has ever suggested that we should have a uniform system of education across Canada. All we have been maintaining for twenty years is that from federal resources there must come the means whereby those poorer and smaller provinces at least can bring their educational standards up to that which will be suitable for all of Canada.
Federal aid to education as implied in this resolution is the only means I know of whereby that thing can be achieved. This is important. The kind of education that boys and girls in one province get is of interest to every other province in Canada. The mobility of our people in Canada, where one out of every three moves from the province in which he is educated into some other province and becomes a citizen of that province, makes it essential that the nation as a whole should assume some responsibility for seeing that an adequate standard of education is maintained in all our provinces.
On this point the Rowell-Sirois report has this statement to make:
The most economically distressed areas are the ones least capable of supporting these educational services, and yet are also the ones in which the needs are likely to be greatest. Not only national duty and decency, if Canada is to become a nation

at all. but equity and national self-interest demand that the residents of those areas be given average services and equal opportunities.
In the modern age contact and intermingling of the population between favoured and unfavoured regions is bound to occur. The more fortunate areas cannot escape the pressure on their standards and the effect on their people; in this case prevention, in both fiscal and human terms, is much cheaper than the cure.
I believe I should pause here to say that the teachers federation, home and school clubs, trustees associations from all across the country, and numerous other organizations, have for many years been pressing for government aid to education at the elementary as well as at the secondary and university levels. The government's reluctance, as indicated this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), to support elementary and secondary schools is usually ascribed to the alleged limitations imposed by section 93 of the British North America Act. That section states that in and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education. Those of us who support federal aid at the elementary and secondary school levels feel that there is no conflict whatever with that clause, which gives the provincial legislatures the exclusive right to make laws in relation to education. There is no conflict in the federal government giving financial support.
It is quite clear from the act that its intention was to place the administration of education under provincial jurisdiction. Most authorities on constitutional law and on education are agreed that financial assistance can be given in such a way that it need in no way whatever encroach upon provincial administration or provincial rights. The report of the Alberta royal commission on taxation in 1948 supports this position, because at page 65 of that report we read this:
There are nine provinces in Canada, each with an educational standard which is within its ability to support. Some no doubt can establish a minimum standard of education beyond the reach of less favoured provinces. The most economically distressed areas are the ones least capable of supporting education and yet they are the ones in which the needs may be greatest. It appears to the commission that there is a place for interprovincial equalization of educational opportunity. This would mean the creation by the dominion government of an interprovincial equalization fund to be distributed among the provinces according to need for the purpose of providing equal educational opportunity to all the children of all the people of all the provinces.
Then the royal commission goes on to say:
The commission if of the opinion that there is no legal hindrance to the dominion in establishing such a fund and further the commission believes that no infringement of the rights of the province need take place in the administration of such fund.

The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) appears to be of the same opinion- at least he was of that opinion in 1945, when he took part in a public debate in Montreal, held under the auspices of an educational association. On that occasion he was reported as having said:
But the constitution does not prevent the federal government from giving substantial assistance to education. Direct assistance might be given in different ways.
I do not know whether he has changed his point of view on that matter since or not. In the brief submitted by the government of Saskatchewan to the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, they go much further and say:
It is submitted that even if the British North America Act were inconsistent with federal financial participation in general education, the federal government should, in, the interest of the national welfare, find means of making such participation possible.
The federal government has given valued assistance in many special aspects of education. In a speech in this house on November 5 of last year I reviewed the entire field and pointed out the extent to which the different departments of government and the various government agencies were already contributing to many specialized phases of education. For instance, the government is helping finance health education across the country. The government is helping finance physical fitness education. It is helping to provide scholarships at the university level. Health education and physical fitness education are subjects which are taught in the elementary schools of this country. Many of the scholarships given by the federal government are given to pupils who are pursuing arts courses in our universities. These arts courses do not specifically qualify students for particular professions such as medicine, law or engineering. In these courses the students receive	a general	education,	andthey are assisted in that by the federal government. As a matter of actual fact the federal government is today in the field of education at the elementary and secondary as well as at university levels. Regardless of any limitation which may be placed upon the government	by	reason	of the BritishNorth America	Act, this government	hasalready entered	that	field.
There appears to be no constitutional barrier to prevent the same government from bearing a share of the financial responsibility for general elementary and secondary school education. In either of those fields the government can give much more effective help to future citizens of this country.
Education
I submit that financial assistance to general elementary and secondary school education would not only be more effective but would be much more democratic than the aid being given in specialized fields by the present government, and on the dollar-matching basis. The dollar matching basis on which money grants for specialized educational services are given today is predicated on the proposition that to him who hath shall be given. It is most helpful to the wealthiest provinces while the provinces in most direct need of assistance find it difficult to match the federal grant dollar for dollar. In many instances the less fortunate provinces cannot take full advantage of these grants and at the same time maintain a maximum effort in the field of general education. There is always the danger that in attempting to avail themselves of federal money they may jeopardize the welfare of children in the field of general education.
When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) suggests that the only way in which the federal government can assist education is by making grants to the provinces to do with as they please he is just not being realistic. That is not the way in which this government is making and has in the past made grants in aid of education and in aid of many other services. The money given to the provinces for health services and hospitalization is not given to be spent as they please; that money is given to the provinces for a specific purpose, to be spent for a specific purpose. The money given to the provinces by this government as a contribution toward old age pensions is not given to be spent as the provinces please; that money is given with a string on it, and that string is that the money shall be spent for old age pensions.
The money that is given in the form of grants to technical schools and which has been of great importance across the country is not given to the provinces to do with as they please. These grants are given with a string attached, that the money must be used for specific purposes. When the Minister of Agriculture suggests that we are introducing a new principle, that there is to be a changed procedure, he is not being realistic, nor is he facing up to the situation that actually exists in connection with grants made to the provinces for these various purposes.
I suggest, as have other speakers, that this house should adopt this resolution as a starting point before the dominion-provincial conference meets in the fall. Educational authorities, both provincial and municipal, have asked that this subject be placed on
