Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a minute or two, not because this subject is not important but because I am anxious to have the motion come to a vote. I hope the resolution will be passed tonight. I think the inequality of educational opportunity which exists in Canada is admitted by practically everyone. A great deal has been said today about inequality which exists as between provinces, and I shall say no more in regard to that, but in my opinion even greater inequality exists as between the urban and rural areas.
I think the provinces could do more than they have done to remove that type of inequality. It costs a considerable amount of money and a good deal of progress has been made in providing more opportunity for children in rural areas, particularly in the newer areas located long distances from towns and where the children are under serious disadvantage. We should do our utmost to remove that type of disadvantage.
Of course the attainment of complete equality of educational opportunity is just not possible. However, the ideal of complete equality of opportunity is one that we should always keep before us and constantly work toward. The desirability of some equalization of opportunity is almost universally admitted, although this afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) seemed to have some doubts about it. He appeared to try to give the house the impression that the people who were supporting this resolution, the people who were working toward federal aid for education wished to have the federal government control the curricula in the different provinces and make all of us alike. There is no thought of trying to make people in one part of Canada a carbon copy of the people in another part. The giving of federal grants to the provinces to help them with their educational problems need not and I do not think will work toward that end.
Let me give an example. The same amount of money might be spent on obtaining an education in a higher institution of learning but yet turn out totally different products. One man might want to specialize in history and spend live, six or more years attending university and taking post-graduate courses. Another man might go in for moral philosophy. Those two men get totally different kinds of education and it would be a brave man indeed who would say that the one was better educated than the other. You fMr. Noseworthy.]
can have the same sort of thing on the provincial level where one province has a different curriculum from another, yet excellent results are produced in each province.
At the present time the main burden of providing for junior and secondary education falls on the property owner in the city or country. That burden has become constantly greater and has now reached the point where in a large number of municipalities it is not going to be possible to increase it very much. Some of the provinces have given a certain amount of help but the provinces have limited sources of revenue and in some cases, probably, not a great deal more help can be given.
Under those circumstances the only means by which a further equalization of educational opportunity can be accomplished is by federal grants to the provinces for that purpose. In my opinion there are three ways in which the federal government could aid in connection with the whole question of education. The first is by means of direct grants which the provinces could use to improve their educational set-ups. The second, which has been mentioned already, is by way of scholarships. This form of aid is being carried out to a certain extent at the present time by way of fellowships granted by the national research council. However, a great deal more could be done in that connection, particularly in the way of training nurses. Assistance in this connection could be provided by grants from the dominion government. At the present time there is a definite shortage of nurses in Canada, and from what I can learn the number of girls entering nursing schools is not nearly sufficient to meet future demands. Having in mind the national health schemes about which the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been talking, that is one way in which some direct aid can be given immediately so far as training and education are concerned.
A third way in which the dominion can help in educational matters is by dominion operated and financed schools. This is not a new idea. We have had dominion operated schools in this country for a long time. I refer to the Royal Military College at Kingston, and its counterpart on Vancouver island, Royal Roads. These dominion schools give specialized training to people who hope to enter the permanent forces of Canada as officers. In addition to military training they provide an extremely good general education. In my opinion that principle should be more widely followed. There is just as much necessity in the national interest for certain other specialized types of schools as there is for the military schools which we now have. Certain types of education and training attract a very small number of people, and there is probably need in Canada for only one

school of that type. Where that situation exists it seems to me that the proper body to operate such a school is the federal government, and it should then permit people from all parts of Canada to attend by means of scholarships.
Something has been said about the supply of teachers, and I should like to say a word on that matter. In the province of Alberta there are a considerable number of schools for which there are no teachers, and the same situation exists in other provinces. Children are taking courses by correspondence, and of course there are unqualified teachers in a large number of schools. The shortage of teachers will increase rather than diminish as long as the present scale of teachers' salaries continues. You cannot expect to attract to the teaching profession the type of men and women needed in that field when the scale of remuneration is considerably less than that of a good carpenter or bricklayer at the present time even for the higher paid members of the teaching profession, to say nothing of the lower paid members who of course receive a great deal less than a skilled workman of any kind. In order to secure for the teaching profession the type of people required and to keep them there after they have been secured, there is no doubt that teachers' salaries must be increased. The time has come when that increase can only take place through the use of federal funds to some extent in aid of education.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that members of the house will all agree that the discussion introduced by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has given us an opportunity to focus our attention on a matter that is of great interest in the country. I think, however, that it would be well at this time to point out that, while most of the speakers have directed themselves to the general purposes which the hon. gentleman had in mind, not all of them have directed themselves specifically to the actual terms of the resolution before the house. For that reason, it may be useful to recall to hon. members what the actual terms are. It provides:
That in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces-
These significant words should be noted:
-for that purpose.
What do the systems of education in our ten provinces involve? They involve the teaching of our children in four categories of education, in some provinces the kinder-55946-1734
Education
garten, in all provinces the primary school, in all provinces the secondary schools, and in all provinces colleges and universities. The policies of education in those fields deal not only with curricula and salaries of teachers but with a whole series of questions which would have to be considered if any proper appraisal of the extent of the financial assistance proposed were to be taken into account.
I think it is important to bear these facts in mind. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) spoke of the assistance now being given by various departments of the federal government. I will come to that later. What I want to point out is that the kind of assistance which he has outlined is not the kind of assistance envisaged by the resolution. We are asked to provide ways and means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose. The grants that are made in various fields now by the federal government are not made for that particular purpose. They are made for specific purposes, and the resolution does not deal with .specific purposes. It deals with the whole question of education in its generalized form.
Apart altogether from proceeding with the consideration of this matter in an orderly way, there has been appointed, as has already been mentioned in this debate, the Massey commission. In speaking about the Massey commission the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), expressing the view of the government on February 3, 1949, stated:
We feel that survey-
He was referring to the survey to be undertaken by the Massey commission.
*-can be made most effectively by a group of Canadians who are Independent of the government. That is why we are going to set up the royal commission I mentioned earlier.
Having in mind the character of the briefs that have been placed before the Massey commission from the universities' conference, the secondary school teachers association and other bodies interested in education, of what value and significance would it be for us, covering this wide field of education, to exercise at the present time a judgment in respect of a matter which certainly has not been finalized in the judgment of the Massey commission?
That is stalling.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
When my hon. friend spoke I listened to him with great attention. I know he is going to give me the same kind of attention because I propose to deal with the matter as seriously as I know how. Speaking on this question some time ago

Education
the Prime Minister said that we recognize the importance of this matter. He used these words at page 946 of Hansard of October 19, 1949:
Personally I have no doubt that it will be necessary to find some way in which these institutions can continue to be supplied with that which is necessary to them to maintain that high standard in their educational activities.
What institutions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The institutions of learning covered by the resolution then before the house, and which is again before the house today.
Now I mention that statement because the speech of the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) lends itself to the interpretation that, because the Minister of Agriculture speaking for the government today had indicated what we thought should be the way in which the resolution should now be treated, we on this side of the house were not interested in education. Those were practically his words. Surely, that cannot be substantiated by the statement which I have just read from the Prime Minister, from the speech which was made this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and from what I know must be accepted as the common view of every member in this house. We look upon education as one of the fundamental requirements of our Canadian society.
In his speech this afternoon, the leader of the opposition-if he would allow me to say so, I thought it was a good one-told us he preferred to give the resolution the interpretation which he wanted; that was his right. He went on to inform the house that we are to have a dominion-provincial conference in the autumn of this year, and this matter should be considered at that time. In that connection, I looked up the words the leader of the opposition uttered when this resolution was discussed last session. Those words deserve repetition tonight. At page 942 of Hansard for October 19, 1949, he said:
For that reason I have stressed, both in this chamber and elsewhere, the urgent necessity of calling a dominion-provincial conference to consider the whole relationship between the dominion and provincial governments so the financial requirements of the provincial governments for all purposes may be fully considered and the amount required to provide adequate educational opportunities may therefore be determined with some knowledge of what is required by each province for that particular purpose.
Surely that is the underlying reason why the attitude taken by the government in this matter should be supported. There is to be a conference at which this matter may be

discussed. No hon. member tonight has suggested a particular plan for giving financial assistance to the provinces, beyond the mere general declaration that, because of the high cost of education, some financial assistance should be given.
Then, in that same debate, the leader of the opposition made this statement at page 943 of Hansard:
I can say most definitely from my own experience-
And he had experience as minister of education in the province of Ontario.
-that the fact that the attempt was made in this case to exercise control by an indirect method is an indication that, in providing for grants of this kind, there must be a definite understanding that the independence and discretion of the provincial departments of education will be retained, no matter what the amount of the grants may be.
He was referring to the grants in aid of physical fitness. This raises the important question of jurisdiction.
You will have to vote for the resolution after what you have said.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That raises the important question of jurisdiction. Some hon. members say that a mere grant in aid, not given for a specific purpose, is not an interference with section 93 of the British North America Act, which assigns to the provinces exclusive competence in matters of education. Having in mind the very caution which the leader of the opposition asked us to note; knowing what was said in this house in the debate last fall when this subject was discussed; recalling the words of the premier of the province of Quebec; knowing how jealously, and properly so, the provinces regard the education field; if this resolution were passed in the form in which it is now before the house, we would create in the minds of the people in several provinces the definite judgment that matters, which at the conference last January were regarded as being included among those rights which were to be entrenched, were likely to be invaded by the central government. Under no circumstances should this parliament do anything which would give any section of our population the impression, rightly or wrongly, that we intended to adopt functions and policies that would violate one of those entrenched rights, education.
Entrenched is right; dug in solid.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend may take that view, but the fathers of confederation laid down the dogma, if you will, that education was a matter for the provinces. Anyone who would interfere with that, after considering the character of this federal state today,

would be doing a great disservice, not only to the cause of national unity but to the cause of education itself.
Let me give an example of the importance of this. All of our provinces have now entered into an agreement with the dominion government with respect to the National Physical Fitness Act, under which grants are made to the provinces to enable them to carry on the work of recreation, handicrafts, and so on. One province has withheld its decision about entering into such an accord. Why? On the ground that in its judgment it jeopardizes the position granted to the province by the B. N. A. Act, and even collaboration on this level is construed by them as an invasion of a field specifically given to them in the British North America Act.
Do you agree with that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not agree with that interpretation, and it is because I do not agree with that view that I have made a distinction between the grants in aid we are now making and the kind of financial assistance which is suggested in the terms of this all-embracing resolution.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend says "explain". Have I not make myself clear? This resolution as it now reads calls for financial assistance, but not for a specific purpose; it calls upon this parliament to take ways and means, without reference to the provinces, to do a perfectly laudable thing, to equalize educational opportunity in Canada. The resolution calls for just that. It does not request us to sit down with the provinces and discuss the desirability of giving them financial assistance in providing an opportunity for improved education, or to help them formulate a policy, or to discuss financial assistance in the whole field of education. Speaking personally, I am not saying that that might not, in some respects, after consultation with the provinces, be a good thing. What I am saying is that to do that merely by the present resolution would be injurious to the national unity of this country.
I know something of how jealously some provinces, and some groups within each province, look upon education as something that has a provincial character, and consequently one that must be so strong in its text as not to permit violation or intervention from a government outside of the province. It is because of that that I think a distinction must be noted between what is desired and how that desire may be realized.
Education

Will the minister permit a question? Does the minister recall a statement made in a speech in Montreal several years ago by his colleague, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), in which he said:
The constitution does not prevent the federal government from giving substantial assistance to education. Direct assistance might be given in different ways.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not disagree with that statement at all, but that is not what this resolution calls for.
It is, precisely.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am going to deal with that. My hon. friend said there was a difference between the attitude taken by the Minister of Agriculture in this matter, and the attitude I took with regard to another matter now before a committee of this house. Surely, that is not an analogy at all. The matter which is before the other committee is one over which this parliament not only has the right to exercise jurisdiction, but actually does exercise jurisdiction in co-operation with the provinces. The terms of the resolution as it is now before the house do not call for specific grants within the meaning of the definition given by the Minister of National Defence in the speech he made in Montreal.
What would happen to this resolution if I had made a specific recommendation for the expenditure of money for federal aid?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Answer that one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Perhaps before I am through I might suggest to my hon. friend that the resolution, if it had been couched in different language, might have provoked a different reaction. My hon. friend laughs, but that is what I honestly believe to be the case.
Not from you.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
There is not anyone in this house who does not want to see the children of this country given the best of educational opportunity. There is no one in this country or in this house who does not want our children to receive, regardless of his or her financial status, the best education possible. In that connection, in spite of the limitations of our educational systems in this country, I think we have every reason for being proud of our achievements. The work that is carried on by the primary schools, by the secondary schools and by our colleges and universities deserves the commendation of every member of this house, as it is freely given. One recognizes the inadequacy perhaps of the income paid to certain teachers in certain sections of the country. Those are all problems that one recognizes; and the fact that

Education
one points out that under the constitution the responsibility for adjustment of those matters resides with the provinces should not and cannot fairly be taken as being opposed to what undoubtedly the hon. member had in mind but which, in actual terms-if I may say so with respect-he has failed to state. It should not be forgotten that for specific purposes we are now doing a great many things in aid of education in one form or another. But for specific purposes nothing that has heretofore been done has been done with the purpose of formulating policy or of dealing with the basic fundamentals of education in any province, but by way of supplemental assistance for specific purposes.
This afternoon the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke of the need for research and in what he said I fully concur, as I am sure every other member of the house will. The work of the national research council in varied fields is a work that assists in a supplemental way the work carried on by our higher institutions of learning in this country. The work of individual departments of government; the encouragement of research in a particular field by the Department of Resources and Development and by the Department of Agriculture; grants given in aid of technical education in this country; the student scholarships under dominion-provincial agreement carried on under the operation of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell); the training opportunities given to veterans, some 133,000 of them, to improve their college and university training as well as to give them vocational training-those are all various steps that indicate the great contribution that is made by the federal government of Canada for the purposes of supplementary education for specific purposes, and I underline the words "specific purposes", to point out that there is >a distinction between grants in aid for a specific purpose and a resolution so all-embracing as this particular one is.
Then there are the grants for social work by the Department of National Health and Welfare; the vocational training grant; the grant for physical fitness; the national research council grant for general purposes, not only for industry, not only for physics, not only for the pure sciences but for medicine and so on. These grants are indeed of a significant character. The national research council fellowships which enable hundreds of our best trained scientists to carry on their research projects in this country at our universities and colleges are a definite contribution in a supplementary way to the cause of education in this country.
I particularly have an opportunity of knowing something of the working of these grants or these fellowships under the medical divi-

sion of the national research council. Under the national health program there has been tremendous assistance-in restricted fields, admittedly, and for specific purposes-to over 2,000 individuals in the past year and a quarter. The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) spoke a moment ago of the need of professional training for nurses. As we know, under the national health program one of the grants is for that very purpose, and under that grant a great number of individuals have received nursing training, and occupational therapy training; and a whole series of other training programs have been accorded to nurses and to persons in corollary positions under that grant. There is the grant under the national health program that is [DOT] given to assist students who are studying _ psychiatry and who are taking a psychology course such as the one that is being carried on at the university of Toronto, and McMaster university. Those are all significant grants that are being made to the cause of education.
When one thinks of the provision that is made under that program for the purchase of teaching equipment, in thousands of dollars in every one of our provinces, one cannot ignore the fact that this is an important assistance to the cause of education. The amount of money that has been given to the provinces under this program for the purchase, for instance, of motion picture machines alone in order to carry on visual education, would run into many thousands of dollars, and must all be regarded as a significant contribution for a specific purpose to the cause of education. The fact that moneys have been given to assist teachers to carry on certain of these courses is not without its significance. The grants made for research under the public health grant, under the t.b. grant, are all grants made in aid of research and extremely important research. Two years ago, on the medical side, there was not more than about $5,000, apart from the national research council grants, given by the federal government in aid of medical scientific research. Today there is almost $2 million available, through this program or through the national research program, by which medical research is carried on. In the field of cancer-an important phase of the work carried on by our medical schools, and that is part of our job of education-two and a half years ago there were three fundamental cancer projects only under way. Today there are over eighty-one as a result of this program and of the assistance given to it by the provinces. Apart from the grants that are made under the specific grants, there is the research grant in this year in the amount of $300,000 which is alio-

cated for the specific purpose of medical scientific research. All these things are not without the greatest value. Any hon. member can today go to McGill university, to the university of Montreal, to Western university or to the university of Manitoba, and he will find there that extremely important research is going on with regard to cortisone and ACTH, two of the most important drugs to appear within the last decade and a half. These are all significant contributions that are entailing tremendous expenditures on the part of the people of this country, all part of the program of assistance supplementarily given to the provinces in respect of matters of research which but for this assistance would in all probability in most instances not be carried out at all.
Then there is another important contribution made by the federal government with respect to education. I am sure the leader of the opposition will agree with me when I say-and he has had experience as minister of education-that after the introduction of family allowances in the province of Ontario, as in other provinces, the school attendance was in greater measure than at any time before in the history of this province. I have been told by the ministers of education in at least four provinces that as a result of the introduction of family allowances the statutory requirement has been lived up to to a greater extent-in one case the figure was 14 per cent higher-than before family allowances were introduced. One should not just accept these family allowances as having merely a social benefit. They have a great benefit in terms of giving the parents the opportunity of keeping their children at school until the statutory school age is reached, and that is a result of great importance.
This year we are spending over $300 million in family allowances.
In what province was that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: In the province of Prince Edward Island.
They both went to school.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That province has a very great educational achievement in spite of its small population.
The family allowance can be regarded as an assistance to education in a way that does not contravene the constitution of our country. The books, the clothing, the nutritional opportunities, all of which enable the child to continue at school, surely must be regarded by this house as a definite contribution towards buttressing the systems of education
Education
that we have in our country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that I express what might be regarded as the reconsidered views of even the hon. gentleman who introduced this resolution when I say, in the language of the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. St. Laurent), speaking in this house on this same motion on October 19 last, as recorded at page 947 of Hansard:
I should think it would be wise not to attempt to determine with any degree of precision how the purposes can best be served until we have-
-heard from the Massey commission, and I would add, using the direction given by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), until we have had an opportunity first of sitting down and discussing these matters in detail with those jurisdictions of government which, under the constitution, have the exclusive responsibility in matters of education.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this resolution, which I support. No fewer than five school boards in my constituency of York West have passed resolutions and written to me on this very matter. The costs and the problems of education in the densely populated and rapidly growing urban municipalities of Ontario require immediate and most urgent consideration from the federal administration.
To give the federal government some idea of their responsibilities, expressed on a cash basis, may I say that in the next few years the suburban municipalities around the city of Toronto will probably have around 10,000 new houses erected by the federal government agency of Central Mortgage and Housing alone. This depends on a number of factors which I will not go into at the moment; but that is the sort of problem and the size of the problem with which we are faced.
Let us look at what this means to the urban municipality and to the school boards. In the next four or five years 10,000 houses will be built in suburban Toronto under the auspices of the federal housing authority. That means that there will be in the neighbourhood of 20,000 children of school age who will require 400 school rooms. The cost today of an individual school room in central Ontario, or in Toronto, runs anywhere from $35,000 to $50,000, depending upon whether it is a primary school or a technical school. That will mean for the national housing project alone an expenditure of some $16 million for schools. The municipalities are in no shape financially to meet this capital cost. What will happen is simply this. You have your federal government assisted houses and you have another group of houses infinitely greater than the federal government assisted houses which in the next five or ten years will probably entail an expenditure approaching $50 million in the Toronto

Education
area alone for new schools. That is new capital for new schools.
The mayor of Toronto has said that today municipal taxation has reached the absolute bearable limit. I would say that if municipal taxation goes up you will begin to have a destruction of the value of real estate either in terms of value or in the security of tenure.
In my opinion the federal government has a direct responsibility for the results of its action in building these housing schemes. Today you cannot build houses without due recognition of the problems of servicing them. One of the most expensive problems of servicing houses is looking after the educational needs of the people who live in them. Today the cost of education is 60 per cent or 70 per cent of the total tax on real estate. If this goes higher two things will happen. First, municipal taxation will increase to a point where the ownership of real estate, home ownership itself, will become less desirable. Secondly, you will put on the municipality a burden of taxation which will seriously jeopardize its solvency. Those are the immediate problems we have to solve. It is not a problem we have to solve five years or ten years from now, but rather jone we shall have to solve this year. Every new house that is going to be built this summer creates its own school problem. Every new house that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation builds creates a school liability which, in my opinion, is the responsibility of the federal administration.
I am not going to go into arguments about the wording of the resolution. Possibly it might have been worded somewhat differently so as to make it suitable to merit my absolute and unqualified support, because I feel that the mere expenditure of money without certain safeguards or qualifying conditions is unwise.
I should like to mention one condition which I think is an important one, and that is that if the federal government is to spend money on education, and I sincerely hope they do, the government must see-if the money goes into capital in the nature of schools which, I believe, is perhaps the most pressing need-that its investment is secure. One of the conditions I would urge upon the federal government, particularly in dealing with new school sections, is to see that the community in which a school is built is properly planned. Today one of the great problems in connection with education, and the cost of it, is that it has been found that the population in the centre of our major cities, and which supported the old schools, has moved out, with the result that those schools serve a diminishing number of pupils. Indeed, we have cases in Toronto where

schools have actually been closed or put to other uses for that reason.
This is an uneconomical thing to have happen, and it can be prevented from now on by proper town planning and proper zoning. I make the point strongly to the government that all money expended in capital expenditures for schools should have attached to it the condition that such money should go only into those school sections or communities where there are adequate town plans, so that the value of the real estate, the value of the school and the type of the community will remain constant and of high value.
My other suggestion by which the government could give immediate aid to the schools in my constituency is one I have made before. Today the average householder in the Toronto metropolitan area is paying between $185 and $200 in taxation for municipal purposes. Of that amount between 60 and 70 per cent goes for education. I suggest that the government consider immediately allowing that taxation as an expenditure deductible from income for taxation purposes.
Today our municipal tax structure is increasing at an alarming rate. This is true all across Canada. What we have to do immediately is to relieve the burden of taxation on the people who today are paying for the education of our children, namely the property owners. I suggest the first thing to be done is to allow school taxes-as a matter of fact, all municipal taxation-as a deduction from income for tax purposes.
That falls into line with the principle of doing away with double taxation. I strongly suggest that the government consider that at once, and that it certainly be considered as one of the principal items to be taken up before the dominion-provincial conference. This is not an academic problem; it is not a problem that can wait for the report of the Massey commission. The commission may sit for years; we do not know. This is not something we can wait for a conference or a royal commission to decide upon. This is something that today in this very year every householder, every owner of real estate and every head of a family is finding right on his doorstep in the demand for taxation for municipal purposes.
Unless this constantly increasing cost of municipal taxation is arrested we are going to find ourselves in a position similar to that of the twenties and thirties when the value of real property was destroyed because of taxation, when municipalities became bankrupt and when the vital security of the whole of the Canadian people was jeopardized. I repeat

that this is not an academic subject; it is not a subject which can wait. This is a subject which requires immediate attention.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is hardly necessary for me to repeat what I said on numerous occasions regarding the importance of education in Canada. Nevertheless, I consider it my duty to oppose the resolution now before the house for reasons, or rather for one reason I shall state very briefly.
Let us see first of all how the resolution before the house reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the.government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. members of this house to note the words "for that purpose". They are very important. The motion, as it reads, provides that the federal government will grant financial assistance to the provinces for educational purposes. I wish to draw the attention of the house to the words "for that purpose" for the motion does not ascribe a particular meaning to the word "education" and I must therefore conclude it refers to education in general. Besides, it is clearly implied by the context and I need not repeat the distinctions made just a few moments ago by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin).
If such subsidies were paid to the provinces by the federal government it would be duty bound to keep a constant check on the provinces in order to make sure that payments were being used exclusively for educational purposes. One can imagine, for instance, a central government at a given time made up of men with definite ideas on the meaning of the word "education" and who would demand that the same meaning be adopted by the provincial authority. The federal government could then claim that certain sums paid to a province for educational purposes are being spent by that province for purposes which, in the minds of the members of the federal government, are other than educational. This might be a source of endless difficulties.
You have only to consider what is happening at the present time in the province of Quebec under the leadership of l'Union Na-tionale to see how far that can go. As a matter of fact, under pretence of financial assistance to school boards, the government of that province has deprived them of their administrative and educational autonomy. In my opinion, the
Education
same thing could easily happen in the federal field if financial assistance were to be granted to the provinces by the federal government for general educational purposes, or in other words, for no specific educational purposes.
As far as I am concerned, my respect for the constitution of this country is such that I can surely not agree with the principle of federal grants to the provinces for general educational purposes. Moreover, I hold no brief from my constituents in this matter.
I do regret the absence from this house of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer). I am convinced that he would agree with me on this principle, and that he would be forced to oppose the views expressed this afternoon by his leader (Mr. Drew) and by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), because the attitude taken by them today does not correspond in any way to the attitude they took during the last electoral campaign, when they claimed to be staunch supporters of provincial autonomy. They laugh because they do not understand.
(Text):
The leader of the opposition may laugh, but he who was such a ferocious defender of provincial autonomy proposed this afternoon that the federal government should enter the educational field which under section 93 is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, since there is a Hansard record may I insist that there shall not be such a deliberate misstatement as that which has just been made. I made it perfectly clear, and in words that could not be misunderstood, that no step taken here should imply any intervention in the exclusive jurisdiction over education by the provincial governments. What the hon. member was trying to do was to place on Hansard an impression which was entirely contrary in every way to what I had said, and which he knew to be contrary.

While I was speaking in French I said that any grants for general educational purposes made to the provinces would necessarily give the federal government the right to review the expenditures, and the right to review by the federal government the expenditures by the provinces for educational purposes means that the federal government would be entering the provincial field of education.
Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious-

On a question of privilege-
Again.

It was not without reason that the fathers of confederation specified in section 93 of the British North America Act that education was solely under provincial jurisdiction. That was done in order to protect the rights of minorities. Now as I belong to a minority, I should be remiss in my duty if, like others from this side of the house who are prepared to vote against the motion out of genuine regard for the Canadian constitution, I did not consider myself bound to express my unqualified opposition to a motion which would involve the loss of sacred rights upon which our very survival depends.

Mr. Speaker, my main reason for rising at this time is that the resolution has been before the house and debated at considerable length on two occasions. To the best of my knowledge no member from the maritimes has taken part in the discussions. In order to disabuse the minds of members who may
Education
think that we have no educational problems in Nova Scotia, I feel it is my duty to rise and say something about the resolution. This afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) displayed some very smart footwork. I admire him for it. He stated that the government was anxious to have a vote on the resolution.
Agreed.

At the same time I notice that there are quite a few government members ready and willing to speak. I think the Minister of Agriculture was quite safe in making that assertion. I cannot understand how he can take the position that the wording of the resolution implies controls. It has been read to the house several times. It is plain and simple, and there is not a word in the resolution to suggest that, if it were passed by the house, the federal government would tell the provincial governments in any way how, when and where they should spend the money. The Minister of Agriculture rang the bell for government members in the event of a vote. He told them he was leading the house, and that in so far as he was concerned he would vote against the resolution. That means that it would be voted down. He did so on the ground that the resolution implied control. I like to be fair in these matters, and I do not think anyone reading the resolution can construe it as entering the provincial field of education.
At the same time the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) suggested that if the resolution had been introduced in some other form dealing with specific matters the chances are it might have received favourable consideration. I am sure the minister knows that if that resolution had been presented in any other form it would not have been discussed by this house. If it had been specific, and recommended that this or that should be done, that money should be spent, then it would have been considered that a private member was advocating government expenditure, and the motion would have been ruled out of order. The only form the resolution could take in order to have a discussion is the innocent form in which it is found. It merely asks the government to increase the grants to the provincial governments for the purpose of equalizing educational opportunity across the country.
I believe this afternoon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was misleading his members with his interpretation of the resolution. Of course, he is entitled to do that, but as house leader I believe he was unfair in the attitude he took. I view this

Education
as an extremely serious matter. The teachers union of Nova Scotia has been urging the federal members to act on the matter of federal aid to education. I am going to put one of their telegrams on the record, in order to show why they think education in the maritimes cannot keep pace with the other provinces. They believe it is due to economic reasons, and I think that is correct. This telegram is signed by the general secretary of the Nova Scotia teachers union, and reads as follows:
The educational opportunities for the children of Canada depend in large measure on the wealth of the individual province. Nova Scotia as you know is one of several provinces which is not financially independent. The Nova Scotia teachers union has long favoured federal aid to education, and now this subject has come before the house, we urge that you, in the interest of the children of Nova Scotia, support federal aid to education wholeheartedly.
That is the position taken by the Nova Scotia teachers union, and it speaks for all teachers in that province.
To support the contention that you cannot have equal educational opportunities across the country on the basis upon which the federal grants to the provinces are made, I cite the remarks of the member for Burn-aby-Richmond (Mr. Goode); I believe he put his finger on the problem. Speaking in this debate this evening he told us that he taught in a rural section of British Columbia, and he believed that 50 per cent of the students that went to high schools had no right to be there. Their parents were not financially able to put these children through university if they did graduate from high school. In many cases the parents were not financially able to allow the children to complete high school training. He felt those children should go into vocational schools. He said that the reason for that was an economic one. I believe that is a rather serious statement, especially since it came from a teacher. That is true not only in rural British Columbia but in many of the rural districts right across Canada. It is true not only in the rural districts of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick but in the industrial sections of those provinces.
If you look at the record of the men going into and coming out of the services you will find that thousands of young Canadians who fought throughout the war and returned to this country were not in a position to take advantage of the vocational training offered by the government because they had not completed the eighth grade. If a man had not completed the eighth grade he could not qualify for vocational training under the veterans legislation. Thousands of these men were not able to go through 
the eighth grade, because of the economic conditions that existed across this country in the years previous to the war.
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was speaking, he painted a lovely picture of the assistance the federal government is rendering, not only in the field of education but also in health. I often wonder whether that information is trickling through to the people, and whether the people actually get it. I believe, as a result of my travels through my province, they are not getting it. For example, if there is money on hand in Nova Scotia for educational purposes or to assist a worthy student, how does it happen that several times during this session I have received letters and telegrams from student veterans who are within a couple of months of graduation from a university when their grant has run out? Those boys are not able to spend the next few months in university and graduate with a certificate because they are unable to pay the tuition. Where are the educational grants that go to the province of Nova Scotia? Several of these cases have beefl brought to my attention, and if there are funds on hand in the province they certainly should be used to assist that particular type of case.
Free school books are provided up to the eighth grade. Sometimes its appears to me as if many of the provinces want eighth-grade scholars. They seem to be afraid that if the student goes through university he may become smart enough to threaten them in the political field. There are too many eighth-grade scholars. In my opinion the books used up to the eighth grade are not very expensive and could perhaps be provided by the parents, but after the pupil leaves the eighth grade and goes to high school the books become expensive and the parents cannot buy them. In the final analysis it is the municipal government that takes the beating on this question of education. In my home town, a town of about 28,000, 60 per cent of the total income is spent on schools. This means that 60 cents of every dollar is spent on the upkeep of schools, and the payment of teachers' salaries. This means cutting into other essential services in that town, and I know that many other towns in the province of Nova Scotia are in a similar position.
I am strongly in favour of the federal government having some supervision of the money. When you look back at some of the . dominion-provincial conferences you find the premiers of the provinces taking the position that they will not relinquish this field or that field. They want to keep the prerogatives laid down in the constitution of 1867, when

the world was completely different from the one which now exists. What is it they want to keep? The supervision of the poor, the lame, the sick and the maimed. If the federal government makes a grant for health purposes, it is earmarked for cancer research or cripples.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: As a result of the direct suggestion of the provinces in each case.
I am not so sure of that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am sure that if I give my hon. friend that assurance he will accept it.

I will take the minister's word for it, but I still think someone is fooling him. We remember how the federal government took the bull by the horns when it enacted the Old Age Pensions Act. It was said that any province desiring to take advantage of it could do so. It was not very long until they all did. I think it is completely unreasonable to expect the federal government to pour out millions of dollars to the provinces and then say the federal government should not have a voice in how the money is to be spent.
If the federal government sends money into Nova Scotia or into any other province I believe that they should be in a position to say that that money is to be used for educational purposes. In the case of the student veteran within two months of graduation but who, because he cannot pay that two months' tuition fee, must go out, I believe that funds should be available to assist him. Then with regard to entrance to high school, for economic reasons and because of differentials that exist in standards from province to province thousands of children cannot take advantage of high school. Where a child shows promise and is recommended by his last teacher, I believe that funds should be earmarked for the purpose of assisting that boy, or girl, to go through high school, and I believe that principle should be followed through university. What have we in this country today? We have professional men who should be digging ditches and we have ditch diggers who should be professional men. Education does not necessarily mean that you have brains. It means that you were fortunate in picking your parents and that they had the finances with which to put you through university.
Until you get around to that specific direction in this field of education, I believe you .will always have the difficulties that you now have. On the other hand, the figures or the statistics put on record this afternoon by the member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) in my opinion were quite revealing. From province to province in this country
Education
the standards differ greatly. As to your educational set-up or social service set-up, everything the government has to spend money on to assist people, there will be a differentiation depending on the income of the province. British Columbia has a provincial income of $105 million a year; Alberta, $79 million; Saskatchewan, $74 million; and Ontario and Quebec are up proportionately. But when you go down to the maritimes, you find it is down to nothing through no fault of their own; they are victims of confederation. Until such time as you have ironed out the inequalities that exist in the whole economy across this country, there will be no possible chance of having equality in social services or educational facilities. These things have to be ironed out first.
I strongly suggest that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) might consider this point, and I know that many representations have been made on it. He could assist education if the Family Allowances Act were amended to provide that, in cases in which a boy or girl had reached the age when he or she was coming off the family allowance, it could be continued while that boy or girl was continuing education. The greatest hardship suffered by the parent is in getting the child through high school. That is where the family allowance could be of great assistance. I know that the act does not provide for that assistance, and the administration are adamant that they are not going to make any changes in that direction. While the family allowance is of great benefit now up till the boy or girl reaches the age where he or she comes off it, I know that many cases have been brought to the attention of the minister asking for a continuation of that allowance while the child is continuing education. That is something the minister could do, and do quickly.
Then as to this business of waiting for the Massey commission to report, may I say that I do not think there is any necessity to delay this particular question until the Massey commission reports. What can the Massey commission report to this government that has not been reported by the Rowell-Sirois commission? I am sure that every member of this house who was here in 1940 and secured a copy of that report has read not all of it-because I do not think anyone would ever read it all-but the sections that apply to social security, revision of the constitution, education, and dominion-provincial rights. Most of us went through it. I think that was the most comprehensive report that was ever brought down in this country, covering the whole economy of the country and the field of dominion-provincial jurisdiction. It was

Education
a new constitution. It made recommendations. If they were carried out, there is no necessity for having any difficulties with the provinces; and there would be no necessity for appointing another commission to take evidence on arts, letters, music and so on and so forth. You have the whole thing in that Rowell-Sirois commission report. You spent millions of dollars on it, brought it into the house, and a few of the members read it. It was never publicized, and it was sent to the archives to gather dust. For anyone who wants the real picture of the whole economic set-up and the changes that are necessary in the economy to bring about some measure of equality as between province and province, the evidence is all contained there in that Rowell-Sirois commission report. I say that the minister should take a look at it and go back over it, because I do not think you will ever gather that kind of data again. I think it is one of the best reports ever written in this country.
I think it is time to take action. We still have a chance to vote on this resolution this evening. I should like to see a vote taken but I should like to see the minister or the cabinet and the members on the government side of the house take the position that the federal government will give assistance if the provinces cannot do anything for themselves, if they have not the money with which to promote education, if they cannot do an adequate job in the field of health. And they admit they cannot because they have not done so though they have been at it since 1867. As to any of the benefits where all this money is being spent, when I go back to my own province my impression is that it is much more difficult today to get service than ever before, either in the way of hospitalization, medical attention, education and all the other things that we are spending all that money on. I do not know what happens in the other provinces, but I certainly cannot see any local administrations that are getting their hands on any of that money to perform any services at all. The minister is building hospitals. He went into that matter at great length this afternoon, but I do not think it is germane to this resolution. But there is no use building hospitals if you cannot get into them. You just built a citadel there and put a lot of equipment into it; and unless you have the wherewithal to pay a lot of money, you do not get in, so you are just out in the cold. I know that the average member is in this position. He is plagued from week to week to have this, that and the other thing done. But there is one thing the Minister of National Health and Welfare could do. He could call his organization together tomorrow and say,

"Let us just extend this family allowance to children who are continuing education." That is simple enough. That would be of considerable benefit to a great many widows particularly who badly need it.

Am I to understand that the minister will take under consideration that matter of amending the Family Allowances Act to provide relief where children are continuing education?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We will all be studying these matters with great attention.

I am glad to hear that the minister is paying special attention to that particular matter. In closing, I should just like to say this. I still cannot understand the Minister of Agriculture's interpretation of that resolution this afternoon, because I know he is a man-
You will talk the resolution out, if you keep on.

No. There is plenty of time. The minister is a man who has a keen insight into these matters and he generally gets to the root of things. But on this particular resolution this afternoon I just could not make him out. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode), a teacher himself, interpreted the resolution and advanced some excellent reasons as to why it should be adopted.

I desire to offer a few remarks in support of the following proposed resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
I think the resolution is clear, despite the arguments that have been advanced against it as interfering with provincial rights. I do

Education
not think there is anything of that nature in it. Despite the fact that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) spoke against the resolution, I wish to endorse it wholeheartedly and also the remarks of the speakers in support of it.
This motion was discussed for an entire day last fall, namely on October 19, 1949, and arguments were set forth by my leader, which may be found on page 942, and following, of Hansard. Dealing with the splendid work of schoolteachers he, as minister of education in an Ontario government, rendered splendid service to education in that province which has been referred to by government speakers today. In that respect I might quote one paragraph of his speech last fall which is to be found at page 944 of Hansard. He said:
There is, however, this important consideration; which cannot be emphasized too often. Even if we built in Canada the finest schools that have ever been constructed anywhere, we would have done nothing to advance our educational standards unless those who are teaching in those schools are highly qualified to teach the children that come under their direction. For that reason, wherever the school may be and whatever type of school may be under consideration, the effort of all those concerned with the advancement of education in Canada should be to raise to a level that is in keeping with their responsibility the salaries of those to whom we are entrusting to a considerable extent the whole future of Canada.
There is a lot of meaning in that paragraph. I am sure there is no hon. member in the house who will not admit that at the present time there is great inequality in educational opportunities throughout this nation. In fact in a bulletin issued in 1945 it was shown that the average salary of teachers in one province was $633 while in another province in another part of the country the average was $1,552. Surely that is a tremendous difference in two provinces of this dominion. In 1941, the last year in which the census was taken, there were only 85,000 citizens in Canada with university degrees. At the same time there were in this country 360,000 people between the ages of 6 and 16, that is school age, who were not attending school at all. In my opinion, these figures are alarming.
I spoke on this matter on October 27, when we were discussing the amendment of the constitution, namely, the British North America Act. I think that is in keeping with the suggestion made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) this afternoon; but in view of some of the statements made today I ' want to refer to the Manitoba teachers federation. Their brief has been endorsed by what is to me the greatest and most influential
organization in Canada, namely, the Cana dian Legion. I do not think anybody will dispute that statement either. They said:
A new definition of education which involves the all-round development of the child, and an emphasis on citizenship, make the educational perspective of 1867 and a narrow interpretation of the provisions laid down in respect to education in the British North America Act untenable today.
At another point in their brief they said:
In any plan of federal assistance it would be understood and1 agreed that the expenditure of funds by the government of Canada would in no way be deemed to confer upon any minister or official of the government of Canada any right of supervision or control over any school or educational institution with respect to which any federal government funds are expended.
That should clear up many of the arguments advanced by government speakers today. They have a very fine and lengthy article, but the point that I am most concerned about is the situation in the province of Manitoba from which I come. Cost of education has been a vital issue in the past two years at our annual Manitoba municipal convention, because the municipal officials must find the greater part of the money by a levy on real estate. In fact our municipal corporations in Manitoba find, by a levy on real estate, $3 for every $1 supplied by the provincial government. I am sure that is an antiquated system of financing education in the province. Notwithstanding that situation, the school trustees association of the province of Manitoba made it a vital issue at their last annual meeting. At their last convention, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 25, 1950, in an article headed, "Education minister says he feels Ottawa cannot give much more aid," the following appeared. First of all, what are we to expect from our provincial minister of education if he attends a conference next fall, when he publicly states that the province cannot expect any more aid from the federal government? According to the article he added:
Doubt that the provincial government could go much further in the matter of financial aid to education was expressed Tuesday by Hon. C. Rhodes Smith, minister of education, in an address to 600 delegates attending the 41st annual convention of the Manitoba school trustees association.
I agree with all the remarks made by my colleague the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) on the great burden on real estate brought about by the cost of education. You cannot continue to have a levy on real estate, as we have in Manitoba, for over 75 per cent of the cost of education, and under that system have equality of education. It just cannot be done. I know that in my own municipality -I have referred to this on occasions, and there are many other examples throughout the entire province-a number of farmers along

Education
the Souris river have lost three crops in the last three years and they are now in the process of losing the fourth.
When this land does produce it is the most productive soil anywhere in that part of the country. Therefore it is the highest assessed property in the country. The majority of the taxes levied there are for the cost of education.
Some twenty miles down the river from me in another municipality there are a group of farmers who have lost the last seven crops in that river valley. They are in process of losing their eighth consecutive crop now. On another occasion I pointed out that they are attempting to get permission to sue this government for the faulty and improper construction of dams on the river, because prior to the construction of the dams those people had not lost a crop owing to flooding since the year 1916. Surely under a modern system today we must face up to the situation.
When I spoke last fall I suggested that municipal authorities should be invited to the dominion-provincial conference next fall. In view of what the Minister of Agriculture said this afternoon, I repeat that if this matter is to be discussed at that conference then the heads of the municipal unions should sit in, at least in an advisory capacity.
I have quoted the statement of the minister of education for the province of Manitoba, who does not think that we should even ask for federal aid. In the statement he said he does not think the province can go any further. What can we people in Manitoba expect when he attends this convention and speaks for the department of education in Manitoba? We do not have any municipal authority here. I am serious about the suggestion that they should be here.
There are further observations I should like to make at this time, but I dealt fully with the subject on October 27, and my remarks are to be found in detail at pages 1200 and following. The wish has been expressed by many hon. members that there should be an opportunity for a vote on this resolution tonight. In view of that, in view of the very full statement I made on the same resolution last fall, in view of the fact that my leader has spoken most effectively- and I have pointed out his record as minister of education in Ontario-and in view of the fact that I wish to endorse the resolution wholeheartedly, and will have more to say at another time, not wishing to be accused of standing in the way of the taking of a vote on this very important matter this evening, I will resume my seat at this time.

Mr. Speaker, members on both sides of the house realize the importance of education. I need not draw the attention of the government to this matter, since it has already appointed a commission to inquire into the educational standards of the Canadian people, and the ways and means of improving them. This commission is known as the Massey commission. So far, the manner in which this commission has performed its duties has brought nothing but commendation.
In the meantime, the government has not remained inactive and after having heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) read a list of the grants made to various universities in this country, all will agree that they are endeavouring to promote education in Canada. Allow me to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the assistance afforded to our veterans with regard to education.

I do not wish to speak at any length on this subject. I am opposed to this resolution in its present form because, first of all, it is premature and, second, because it infringes on the rights of the various provinces.

Mr. Speaker,-
Question.

May I assure hon. members that I did not call "question" when they spoke. I shall take only a few moments to speak on a subject concerning which I had prepared copious notes. However, it is not my intention tonight to repeat the arguments made earlier. I believe, as did those who spoke earlier, that this is a matter of great national importance.

In speaking tonight I do so without attempting either to support or to oppose the resolution, but rather to bring out certain points which have not been mentioned before. I do this without in any way trying to twist the words of any previous speakers or to paint any black pictures.
It has been mentioned by several speakers that education is within the jurisdiction of the provinces. There is no point in my discussing that matter further. It is only fair to say however that the national government has been most active in promoting certain phases of education. Our federal government has been most scrupulous in trying to meet its constitutional obligations in respect of the protection of the rights of the provinces and the rights of minorities.
In discussing this matter there are certain points which must be taken into consideration. It has been my hope not only to ask but to answer some of those questions. First, have those who are supporting or who have been opposing the resolution as worded taken into consideration our educational history, particularly with regard to finances, both in the past and at the present time? Have they considered the method by which technical and vocational education were introduced in Canada? Have they considered to any great extent the federal government's present participation in education? Have they thought of the difficulties that occurred in the United States when under W.P.A. they began issuing grants very freely for the building of school plants? Have they thought of the system of scholarships in effect in other countries? Most important, have they thought just what the expression "equal educational opportunity", which has become almost a cliche, really means? Have they thought at what level they would like to have federal educational aid? Is it to be at the primary level, the secondary level or the university level?
Several speakers have made the suggestion that if we were to spend twice or three times as much on education we would have a system twice or three times as good. However, not one of them carried his argument further; each was content to make only the bald statement. I do not see how we can assume that by spending twice or three times as much we shall of necessity have a much better system of education.
I feel I must reply to two or three statements made by members on both sides of the house regarding education in the maritime provinces. I believe I can speak with some little authority-certainly I can so far as education in Nova Scotia is concerned-

because as I said a few days ago I spent practically all my adult life working in the field of education in that province.
When the suggestion is made, as it was by at least one speaker, that Nova Scotia does not have a good educational system, or a system not as good as that in some other provinces, I should like to know by what method we are going to measure the system? Earlier speakers suggested that whether or not a teacher was paid $1,150 in one area and $1,152.40 in another, it did not necessarily follow that the teacher would be any better or that the type of service given would be any better.
It has been said that certain provinces have spent a great deal more for their physical plant and equipment. This is true. But it does not necessarily follow that the education will be better in proportion to the additional amount of money spent. I do not believe it is generally realized-certainly it is not by some who spoke earlier today-that in Nova Scotia we have embarked within the last decade upon a system of improving considerably our physical plant and equipment, in securing better training for our teachers, and planning new types of school buildings we propose to build within the next few years. We plan for approximately seventy-five rural high schools and consolidated high schools, which will mean that practically every boy and girl in Nova Scotia will have rural high school and consolidated school facilities available to them.
We have under construction at the present time two regional vocational high schools. They are being financed partially by grants under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act of 1942. We propose during the next few years, if the municipalities in the areas concerned are as interested in the plan as the counties of Yarmouth and Halifax have been, to build at least three more regional vocational high schools. At the same time we are doing this we are spending much more money on education than we did before. I do not think that any hon. member should stand up in this house and suggest that, because we are not spending as much per capita, as much per pupil or as much in total as some of the other provinces, we have not as good an educational system.
There are several ways in which the dominion government takes part in education. Some have been mentioned and I should like to mention one or two. You may wonder why I go from a discussion of rural and vocational high schools to a discussion of the research council and other such matters, but as I mentioned earlier I do not want to repeat what previous speakers have said. I think the establishment of the research council
